News.title: Shock number of young Brits who are leaving the UK for good revealed – and the countries they are headed
News.content:
YOUTH EXODUS Shock number of young Brits who are leaving the UK for good revealed – and the countries they are headed

TENS of thousands of young Brits left the UK last year — sending net migration ­plummeting to the ­lowest level since Covid.

Official figures yesterday showed 171,000 people were added to the population last year, almost half the number seen in 2024.





The significant drop was driven by tougher visa rules and a big fall in foreign workers coming to Britain.

But the figures also revealed a widening gap between the number of British nationals leaving the UK for destinations such as Australia, and those returning, especially among younger Brits.

In total, 136,000 more Brits left the country than returned in 2025.

Among 16 to 34-year-olds, the gap hit 75,000 — the highest level since the Office for National Statistics introduced its current system for measuring migration.

The ONS said the level of “negative” net migration among young Britons was the “most significant” factor among all age groups of UK citizens.

A spokesman added: “This gap has grown every year since 2022. This may suggest young Brits who move abroad for work are staying for longer periods, or that students who study overseas are then staying for work.”

The number of Brits on working holiday visas in Australia has more than doubled in two years, jumping from around 38,000 to almost 80,000.

The scheme allows young people to live, work and travel Down Under Australia for up to three years.



Poland has also seen more arrivals of British-born people with Polish parents, with numbers climbing from 42,000 in 2015 to 185,000 last year.

The wider fall in migration comes after a major tightening of the immigration system under both the Tories and Labour.

Rules introduced over the past two years stopped overseas care workers and foreign students bringing family members to Britain, and increased salary thresholds for skilled visas.



Labour has also raised English language requirements and cut the length of post-study graduate visas.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood hailed the results, saying: “Net migration has fallen by 82 per cent in just three years.

“We will always welcome those who contribute to this country and wish to build a better life here. But we must restore order and control to our borders.

“As these statistics show, real progress has been made, but there’s still work to do.

“That is why I’m introducing a skills-based migration system that rewards contribution and ends Britain’s reliance on cheap overseas workers.”



But the figures are likely to reignite a bitter civil war over immigration – with dozens of Labour MPs urging the Home Secretary to water down plans to make migrants wait ten years instead of five before gaining permanent settlement rights.

The backbenchers argue the plans are unfair and risk damaging sectors already struggling with staff shortages, including social care.

But allies of Ms Mahmood believe softening the rules would hand Nigel Farage a major political weapon.

An Ipsos poll found 41 per cent of Britons now see immigration as one of the biggest issues facing the country — up nine points in a month.



FIFTH WERE BORN ABROAD ONE in five people in Britain are now foreign-born after an influx of 2.4million in three years. Government data shows that 13.1 million UK residents were born overseas and ­represent 19 per cent of the population. It reflects a spike in net ­migration after the Covid pandemic which experts say has “pushed the foreign-born to its highest ever share of the UK population”. Critics branded it the ­“Boriswave” as they arrived from non-EU countries during Boris Johnson’s time as PM, due to his points-based immigration ­system. “Opponents said the Government has failed to control the numbers arriving. Net migration to the UK reached a record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023 but has since dropped off. Office for National Statistics data published yesterday showed 9.2 million of the foreign-born population in 2024 came from countries outside the EU. Dr Ben Brindle, researcher for the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “The sharp increase in net migration after the pandemic has pushed the foreign-born to its highest ever share of the UK population. “Migration is down now, but the economic impacts depend more on who is — or is no longer — migrating than how many.” Reform UK has vowed to deport hundreds of thousands of migrants who arrived in the “Boriswave”. And Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has pledged to double the period people live in the UK before claiming Indefinite Leave to Remain — from five to ten years.

Economic gloom also remains deep, with nearly three-quarters expecting things to worsen over the next year.

New Home Office data yesterday also showed the number of asylum seekers being housed in hotels has fallen sharply.

At the end of March, 20,885 asylum seekers were living in them, down 35 per cent in a year and the lowest figure since records began in 2022.

However, the Tories warned the problem has not disappeared but instead been shifted into towns and suburbs across Britain.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp also said: “Brits are leaving on a massive scale and non-EU immigration remains far too high.



“Mass immigration undermines our society and low-wage immigration is bad for the economy.

“British families feel it in lower wages, longer waiting lists for public services and housing shortages.

“Labour must go further and reform indefinite leave to remain before their hard-left flank forces them to abandon it altogether.”

The figures also showed the number of foreign-born people in Britain has surged to a record 13.1 million — nearly one in five of the population.

The Home Office last night insisted emigration was not the reason behind the 82 per cent drop of net migration over three years.



It said: “Emigration of British nationals has been flat in recent years. This year it is lower than last year.

“Claims about higher numbers of young Brits leaving are not true either. Emigration in the 16-to-34 age group has been stable.

“Again, it declined slightly in 2025.”

News.title: Leeds white van man was dead right – useless Labour IS ruining Britain and here’s all the ways how
News.content:
ARE you getting excited yet about the Great British Summer of Savings? Is the anticipation tingling through your bones?

Not only will you get a few quid off a trip to Alton Towers, your kids will be able to take buses for free and you’ll enjoy the thrill of saving a whopping 10p on your weekly supermarket shop — all thanks to Rachel Reeves.





But don’t rush out and spend all that extra cash on a new car or bathroom suite just yet, eh?

Because the Chancellor’s promise to do something to help ordinary Brits with the rising cost of living has turned into a Great British Summer of Big Fat Nothing.

No wonder the White Van Man, who shouted at Reeves at a Leeds petrol station, was so angry when he yelled: “You’re ruining the country! You are useless!”

He was right.

People struggling to pay their household bills, worrying about the cost of the weekly shop and keeping their business afloat need real, tangible help, not more gimmicks and sound bites.

The Chancellor’s decision to keep the 5p cut on fuel duty until the end of the year is hugely welcomed (and largely down to The Sun’s campaigning on behalf of hard-pressed readers).

But when it comes to the rest of her offerings, Reeves is falling far short.

If you can afford to fork out to take your family to a theme park or zoo this summer, it will be a tiny bit cheaper after Reeves announced a temporary cut in VAT from 20 per cent to five per cent for the summer holidays.



The discount will also apply to children’s entry to cinemas, concerts, soft play and theatres, as well as kids’ meals in restaurants and cafes.

Which all sounds great, but it will be up to businesses if they pass the tax cut on to customers.

The free bus journeys for children under 15 in August are all very well too, but it isn’t exactly going to pay the rent, is it?

Thankfully, the Treasury dropped its nonsense about a supermarket cap on the price of essential food items.



But the savings from cuts to import tariffs on some basic foods will amount to mere pennies.

And the whole big “giveaway” is going to cost the Treasury about £300million.

Or rather, it’s going to cost you and me that amount — because none of the “free” stuff the Government hands out is actually free. It’s all paid for with our money, taken in taxes out of our own pockets.

We don’t need slightly cheaper days out at Alton Towers, we need grown-up policies that encourage economic growth, reward hard work and aspiration and promote investment in jobs and wealth creation.



There are a whole range of measures the Chancellor could announce which would make a big difference to our economy and our wallets.

How about cutting income taxes or raising the tax rate thresholds so Brits don’t get walloped with 40 per cent income tax just for working hard?

Or what about cutting VAT on all hospitality to help that industry — one of our biggest employers — get back on its feet?

What about cutting employers’ National Insurance — a literal tax on jobs — so that businesses can afford to expand and employ more people?



What about slashing VAT on petrol and diesel at the pumps to cut costs for millions of motorists and the hauliers who transport everything we buy?

How about slashing welfare dependency so our taxes are spent on vital public services, not to fund lazy, entitled 20-year-olds to watch daytime telly?

What about getting rid of the mad Net Zero policies and the billions in subsidies paid to fund unreliable intermittent wind and solar power?

Instead, we’re getting a few quid off a family trip to the cinema. Gee, thanks.



Reeves would be wise to listen to that White Van Man who berated her this week.

She retorted by telling him his bad “manners” were “not very British”.

But I can’t think of anything more quintessentially British than telling our political leaders the truth when they’re doing a rubbish job.

The Great British Summer of Savings is an insult to struggling taxpayers and, after this week, there will be plenty more people queueing up to tell the Chancellor what they think of her policies.

Reeves would be wise not to visit any more petrol station forecourts any time soon.



Migration fall is fake news

DON’T believe the claims of good news about net migration falling.

Once again, the true numbers are being hidden.

The Prime Minister and Home Secretary were busy crowing about a big drop in the latest net migration figures – from a 2023 high of 944,000 during the Boris-Wave to 171,000 in 2025.

But that headline figure does not tell the full story. Not by a long way.



Much of that cut in net numbers (the difference between arrivals and those leaving) is not due to fewer migrants coming to the UK but more Brits and EU nationals choosing to leave the UK.

Last year, some 627,000 non-EU migrants still arrived here, mostly from India, China, Pakistan and Nigeria.

And that’s just the legal arrivals with visas, so doesn’t include the tens of thousands of illegal boat and lorry arrivals.

Taking into account the non-EU migrants who left the UK, that still means an extra 350,000 here more than the year before.

That’s the equivalent of a city the size of Coventry arriving to live here last year alone.



Meanwhile, 246,000 Brits chose to leave our shores, many of them hard-working, bright, ambitious youngsters who are taking their talents (and potential future taxes) with them.

After decades of mass immigration, the foreign-born population of the UK is now estimated to be more than 13million. That’s almost one fifth of the population who were born abroad.

That is a huge, unprecedented and historic change and it’s happened over a few decades.

You’d have to be deaf, dumb and blind not to see that mass immigration has caused huge changes, affecting our economy (not in a good way), schools, housing costs, law and order, culture, community cohesion and our elections and foreign policy.

Yet British voters were never asked if they wanted that change. No one asked them if they wanted mass immigration, and when they told politicians at election after election they wanted numbers cut, they were ignored.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Government, and much of the media, will try to claim these latest migration figures prove this issue has been solved.

The facts tell a different story.

News.title: There’s so much titanium in my head I’m in pain ALL the time, says Victoria Cross-winning Iraq War hero Johnson Beharry
News.content:
HE is one of just seven living holders of the Victoria Cross, yet Johnson Beharry shrugs and shifts uncomfortably when words such as hero and brave are used to describe him.

Today, the bearer of Britain’s highest military decoration will play a central role in the Royal British Legion’s commemorations of the Iraq War at the National Memorial Arboretum, Staffordshire.





Johnson, 46, is among 1,500 veterans and their families gathering to mark the 15th anniversary of the end of the conflict which claimed the lives of 179 British soldiers and serving personnel and left him with life-changing injuries.

He said: “I don’t know what it’s like to be out of pain any more. I’m telling you that while I’m getting goosebumps.

“All of the top of my head is reconstructed, so that’s titanium. My head is quite heavy just to hold up, so my neck and my shoulder feel like constant whiplash.

“I’m tired all the time. I don’t sleep very much, more like a cat nap, and I’ve spent the last 22 years in eight out of ten levels of pain.

“My head hurts constantly and because there’s so much titanium, it’s very heavy to hold up.”

In 2004 Johnson saved the lives of 42 of his colleagues in Iraq, in two attacks weeks apart.

In the first attack, in the early hours of May 1, he was driving a Warrior armoured vehicle which was caught in a fierce ambush involving rocket-propelled grenades, machine-gun fire and roadside bombs.

Despite being wounded and exposed to enemy fire, he drove the damaged vehicle and led four others to safety, then rescued his fellow injured soldiers from the burning Warrior.



In the second attack, on June 11, a grenade hit his Warrior vehicle six inches from his head, causing serious shrapnel injuries, which led to the loss of 40 per cent of his brain.

Today, still serving, and promoted to Warrant Officer Class 1, Johnson is one of 6,000 British personnel who were injured in the eight-year conflict.

Recalling the devastating second attack, he said: “I remember someone removing my helmet from my head, pouring water on me, and saying, ‘Harry, Harry, stay with me’ — and that’s it.



“Everything went off. The next thing I know, I was in hospital in Birmingham.”

According to government figures, last year alone more than 18,000 Armed Forces personnel sought help for mental health problems — and Johnson has had a continuing battle with mental health issues himself. He said: “I think the best person to ask about who I am is my wife, because to me I think I’m OK.

“The minute I step out, I’m professional, I’m a soldier, I’m on duty.

“So no matter how bad my pain is, you will never stop me from carrying out my duty.

“But when I go back home and I take my uniform off, you’d have to speak to my wife and kids and ask them who I am, what kind of person they’re dealing with, because I’m not performing any more when I’m not on duty.



“I’m in that safe place where I can let my guard down.”

Like thousands of serving and former service personnel across the country, Johnson’s mental health is an ever-present issue.

A suicide attempt in 2008 and a diagnosis of PTSD — post-traumatic stress disorder — have meant his recovery has been just as much mental as physical.



He said: “I’m back in rehabilitation. Last year I realised — well, my wife told me — I’m not the person I used to be.

“So I had to do something about it, and I went back into rehabilitation.”

Thousands of former servicemen and women who served in Iraq have been supported by charities such as the Royal British Legion to deal with their physical and mental injuries.

While dad-of-three Johnson is the highest-honoured soldier from the conflict, he is using his position to speak out in support of every man and woman who might now be struggling as a result of their military service.

He said: “I live my life conscious of the problems I have to deal with.



“That is because I haven’t left the battlefield — I feel I’m still there.

“Every time I was injured, I was in the middle of contact, and the last thing my brain remembers is going into that.

“So I would like to go back. I don’t care which country it is — it doesn’t have to be Iraq or Afghanistan, but I need to hear it again.”



He said of coping with everyday situations: “I have to deal with loud bangs, sirens, kids crying.

“It’s a lot, just dealing with day-to-day life.”

He says he has reacted in the past — by getting upset, even fighting people.

Johnson added: “I went into rehabilitation for anger management. I realised the only way to deal with it was to stay conscious.” Although he has a VC tattoo that covers his entire back, Johnson, who proudly describes himself as an infantry soldier, revealed that he does not think about his medal.

He said: “I met a lot of Victoria Cross holders after I received mine. There were 14 of us alive at the time.



“I remember meeting Eric Wilson, VC.

“He was 93 and used to say, ‘I’m 93 years, six months, three days, and 12 hours old’, or whatever it was, which always made me smile.

“At one reunion, I remember counting the room and thinking, ‘I can’t find all 14 Victoria Cross holders’. Then I realised I was one of them.



“That was the only moment I truly thought, ‘Oh wow’. The medal represents my battle group, my regiment, my colleagues, my boys who came back in one piece, those who didn’t come back in one piece, and who didn’t come back at all.

“I wear it with pride, knowing the history it represents, but I’m not connected to it.

“I don’t think about it. I know I have it and I know what it represents but I cannot mentally associate myself with the medal. I just don’t know how to feel about it.”

He is also visibly uncomfortable at being called a hero. He said: “I don’t want to sit here and say, ‘The lives I saved’.

“It was my duty. Anyone else would have done the same.”



When reminded that there are 42 men alive who have children, grandchildren, wives, sisters, mums, dads and brothers who get to tell stories because of Johnson’s bravery, he looked uncomfortable with the praise, shifting in his seat at the National Army Museum in West London during our interview.

He said: “You’re telling me that, and I can feel the emotions in my body, but I don’t look at it that way.

“Every decision I made on the ground was conscious.

“I knew I wasn’t going to die in the process.

“I had no fear of dying because I had ruled it out.



“But when I hear it, it confirms to me I wouldn’t change my pain, my sleepless nights, because yes, there are 42 soldiers and families who got their loved one back.”

With his charity work, plans for a follow-up to his top-selling 2006 book Barefoot Soldier, and the Warrior armoured vehicle that saved his life going on display next month at the National Army Museum, Johnson has a busy schedule.

The soldier has just one day off in the next four months.

There is a mix of excitement and trepidation at being united with the vehicle that changed the course of his life for ever.

Then in November he has been invited by the King to Antigua for the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting.



Yet despite his life changing irreversibly 22 years ago, Johnson is quick to smile and see the positives that life has given him in the years since then.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “The way I deal with life is this — I take all the negative things and turn them into positives.

“That’s how I survive.”

News.title: Army commander left super-sensitive to the cold after he was not given mittens sues MoD for £200k
News.content:
AN Army commander left hyper-sensitive to the cold after he was not given mittens is suing for £200,000.

Darren Stoddart was driving a vehicle with no cover from the elements.





The 40-year-old’s Light Dragoons had been on a tactical training exercise on Salisbury Plain, Wilts, from February to March 2022.

He was issued “ineffective” kit gloves and suffered a non-freezing cold injury (NFCI), say files lodged against the Ministry of Defence with London’s High Court.

Barrister Thomas Banks said: “He often had to drive around in an open vehicle in wet clothing. His hands, in particular, got wet and cold.

“Towards the end of the exercise, his squadron conducted a simulated attack in torrential rain.

“He became soaking wet but had to drive to a distant area.

“He was travelling at speed and exposed to wind-chill. His hands became numb and he lost all dexterity in his fingers.

“When he was able to rewarm his hands, they developed a feeling like he had thousands of tiny cuts all over them and the pain kept him awake at night.”

Mr Banks said Cdr Stoddart, of Hartlepool, has achieved “a degree of ­recovery” but remains cold sensitised.



The injuries ­hindered his promotion chances, it is claimed,

Guidance in 2016 states spare mittens should always be carried, said Mr Banks.

Cdr Stoddart is suing the MoD for negligence.

Its defence was not available from the court.

News.title: Airbus & Air France guilty of corporate manslaughter after pilots slept before 228 people died in crash disaster
News.content:
MAJOR airline Air France and aircraft manufacturer Airbus have been found guilty of manslaughter over a horror plane crash that killed 228.

Five Brits and three Irish doctors were among those who perished in the 2009 disaster – the worst in French aviation history.





Recorded conversations between three pilots revealed David Robert, 37, and Marc Dubois, 58, were asleep during the Paris-bound flight from Rio de Janeiro.

Only the junior pilot, Pierre-Cedric Bonin, 32, was awake when the plane hit a tropical storm.

The AF447 passenger jet stalled during the storm and plunged 38,000ft into the water, killing all on board.

Air France and Airbus were found “solely and entirely responsible” for the tragedy by the Paris Appeals Court.

A court previously cleared the companies in April 2023, but they were found guilty on Thursday after an eight- week trial.

Relatives of some of the passengers, who were mainly French, Brazilian and German nationals, gathered to hear the verdict.

The Airbus A330 vanished from radars on June 1, 2009, and its wreckage was only found two years later after a search over 3,860 square miles using underwater robots.

All 12 crew members and 216 passengers died due to a technical failure involving the jet’s sensors and the pilots’ inability to react to the plane stalling.



The aircraft plunged into the sea at a speed of 11,000ft per minute, French investigators later concluded.

The pilots had been confused by faulty air-speed readings, and mistakenly pointed the nose of the plane upwards when it stalled, instead of downwards.

Black box recordings revealed one of the cockpit crew saying: “Damn it, I don’t have control of the plane, I don’t have control of the plane at all!”



The captain can then be heard saying: “No, no, no… Don’t climb… no, no.”

The co-pilot then says: “Damn it, we’re going to crash… This can’t be happening!”

Seconds later the cockpit voice recorder stops.

Prosecutors accused Air France of failing to provide sufficient training in how pilots should react in case of malfunction of the Pitot tubes, which enable pilots to monitor their speed.

The pilots were proven to have reacted incorrectly when the plane stalled after the speed sensors froze over.



Among those who died on the Airbus was Graham Gardner, an oil worker from Gourock, in Renfrewshire, and Arthur Coakley, an engineer from Whitby in North Yorkshire.

Alexander Bjoroy, an 11-year-old boarder at Clifton College in Bristol, also perished, as did PR executive Neil Warrior.

The three young Irish doctors who died were returning from a two-week holiday in Brazil.



Since the disaster, pilot training on dealing with technical breakdown is said to have been stepped up by Air France.

The companies have been ordered to pay the maximum fine of £195,000 each for the civil offence, despite victims’ families saying it is not enough.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

During their closing arguments in November, the prosecutors said the companies’ behaviour had been “unacceptable”, accusing them of “pouring out nonsense and pulling arguments out of thin air”.

Both Airbus and Air France had repeatedly denied the charges. There may be further appeals due to reputational damage caused.

News.title: Man who brutally beat carer to death with brick then hid her body in his flooding home is jailed
News.content:
SICK ATTACK Man who brutally beat carer to death with brick then hid her body in his flooding home is jailed

A PARANOID schizophrenic has been jailed for a minimum of 12 years for strangling and beating his carer to death with a brick.

The attack was labelled in court as being a “brutal and motiveless” killing.





David Walsh, 35, was found naked and screaming by police who forced entry into his Birmingham home on the night of June 22 last year.

A colleague of carer Irene Mbugua raised the alarm when he had not heard from her, Birmingham Crown Court heard.

Walsh, who has previously been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, ADHD, autism, Asperger’s, learning difficulties and depression, had to be tasered by officers to bring him under control as he spat at and bit them.

Officers then returned to the address in Winson Green on June 23 where they found the body of Ms Mbugua, a mother-of-four, on the floor after removing a sofa that blocked the door to the kitchen.



The kitchen ceiling had partially collapsed on her body after a tap was left on in the bathroom above and flooded the property, Walsh’s sentencing hearing heard on Thursday.

The 46-year-old victim had been strangled and beaten about the head with a brick, which was found in a plastic bag in a bedroom, and had suffered a bleed on the brain and fractures to her skull and ribs.

Walsh told a forensic psychiatrist he had initially strangled his carer before hitting her 10 times with the brick and moving her body downstairs.

Prosecution counsel Michelle Heeley KC told the court Walsh, who had live-in carers stay with him in his home, had stopped taking anti-psychotic medication around three months before the fatal attack.



It is believed Ms Mbugua was killed on the evening of June 21, when screams coming from Walsh’s home were picked up on a nearby CCTV camera.

The day after, Walsh used his carer’s bank card in a local convenience store and JD Sports while she lay dead on the floor at his home.

Neighbours said Walsh was “acting strangely”, grabbing their wrists and telling them to repent their sins and was also heard on CCTV saying: “We are free from death, we are free from pain, we have done what we have done.”

After his arrest, Walsh was not fit to be interviewed and was later charged with murder, but pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility on the second day of the trial at Warwick Crown Court in February this year.

Small amounts of cocaine had been found in his blood following his arrest.



Defence barrister Philip Bradley KC acknowledged the victim’s four children as he addressed the court.

He said: “For any child to lose their mother is an utter tragedy. For that mother to be lost in circumstances such as these makes a terrible situation all the worse.”

He added that Walsh had a “real fondness” for Ms Mbugua as she had “helped him so much”.

Sentencing Walsh, who sat in the dock wearing a dark jacket and a white top, to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 12 years, judge Mr Justice Wall KC said the killing had “devastating consequences” for Ms Mbugua’s family.

He said: “This was a brutal and motiveless killing. The victim was your live-in carer Irene Mbugua, who was employed to assist you because you had mental health difficulties.



“You acknowledge how much help she provided you before you did what you did.

“The harm you caused this family is profound and lifelong.”

He added: “The fact you were able to avail yourself of a defence of diminished responsibility does not mean you bear no responsibility for your actions.”

The judge said Walsh had chosen to stop engaging with mental health professionals and taking his medication, despite knowing it would lead to a deterioration in his mental state.

He said: “You voluntarily took illicit drugs, cocaine, which were bound to have a destabilising effect on you.



“The fact they were present at all is troubling in the case of a man with your mental health difficulties.”

He continued: “You realised what you had done after you had done it. You were not insensible to your actions. That is why you hid her body… and the brick you had used in the attack.

“You took advantage of what you had done by taking her bank card and using it to buy yourself things the next day.”

The judge said Walsh was also in breach of a suspended sentence for attempted robbery in 2021 when the killing happened.

He said: “Your victim was your care worker – she was killed while working and staying in your home and was therefore vulnerable.



“She must have been terrified in the moments leading up to her death.”

The judge accepted the “brutal and unexplained” attack was not premeditated, but said he had no doubt Walsh was a dangerous offender.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Walsh was also sentenced to four months to run concurrently for each of the four counts of assaulting an emergency worker he admitted to after leaving two police officers with bite marks and another with bruising and a cut lip.

At the end of the sentencing hearing, the judge offered his “deepest condolences for the terrible loss that has been sustained” by Ms Mbugua’s family, adding: “It is unimaginable.”

News.title: Huge queues clog up Mount Everest’s ‘Death Zone’ as record number of climbers scale mountain in a single day
News.content:
HUGE queues are clogging up Mount Everest’s “Death Zone” as the highest mountain on earth is hit with a record season of climbers.

Pictures and video from those scaling the icon show dozens of people standing in a row with their climbing gear on as they wait for those in front of them to move forward.





A new record was set on Wednesday as 274 climbers scaled the mount from Nepal, beating the previous peak of 223 on May 22, 2019.

It was the highest number of successful ascents from the mountain’s south side in a single day.

Good weather and massive waiting lists are behind the big numbers.

In April, a 100ft-high ice block shut down the route – ballooning waiting times.



So-called “ice-fall doctors” worked for several weeks to clear a path which opened on May 13.

The Nepalese Department of Tourism said: “A major obstruction – a large unstable ice serac in the Khumbu Icefall – has been safely addressed following detailed assessment and adherence to safety protocols”.

“As climbers navigate the route, utmost caution is urged, particularly in the serac-affected section. Wishing all a safe ascent.”

Nepal issued nearly 500 permits to climb the world’s highest peak this year.



But there is only a narrow window of time during which people may attempt the climb, from late April to the end of May.

The ice-block delay sparked the soaring numbers of Wednesday.

“The main reason for the queues is simply that there are more people climbing the mountain,” Tim Mosedale told The Telegraph.



The British expedition leader has scaled Mount Everest seven times.

Mosedale, who has 25 years of experience climbing in Nepal, said: “There are more and more people with a drone and an Instagram account who are looking for content”.

He added: “If you have unfit or incompetent people on the mountain, then they are putting the lives of Sherpas at risk. There are a lot of people who are out of their depth, who don’t realise how close to the edge of safety they are”.

Wealthy climbers are demanding extra oxygen tanks – each of which must be carried up on the back of a Sherpa – and so clogging up the mountain further.

An ascent up Everest with bonus oxygen costs between £52,000 to £72,000 per person.



The tanks are needed to keep breathing at the extremely high altitudes of over 26,000ft.

Oxygen levels in the mountain’s “death zone” are extremely low and one small mistake could lose you a finger – or your life.

Accidents are common on the world’s highest mountain and the overcrowding increases risks of death.



One mountaineer who took his glove off for just a few minutes on top of Mount Everest paid a high price for his mistake.

Madhusudan Patidar, 29, removed the glove for four minutes in freezing -35°C conditions on the mount’s “death zone”.

The split-second decision cost the climber his finger.

The 29-year-old from India shared details of the harrowing ordeal with followers online.

“Somewhere above 8,000 metres I briefly removed my outer glove to adjust my camera equipment,” he said.



“It was a small decision. Four minutes with a bare hand at -35°C with wind chill.”

It recently emerged that Everest guides are secretly poisoning climbers to cash in on lucrative insurance schemes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The con reportedly works by getting climbers to stage a fake medical emergency and calling expensive rescue helicopters.

News.title: UK heatwave live: Met Office forecasts 33C weather as four regions face heatwave
News.content:
Met Office weather forecasters expect an official heatwave to be declared in four parts of the UK over the Bank Holiday weekend as record-breaking 33C temperatures loom

The Met Office expects an official heatwave as temperatures rise to 33C over the Bank Holiday weekend.

Forecasters from the national weather agency say the mercury could rise as high as 30C on Saturday, 32C on Sunday, and 33C on Monday. This would mean we see the hottest ever temperature for May, as the current record is 32.8C.

The south-east of England is expected to be the hottest region, although official heatwave conditions could also be reached in central England, western England and parts of Wales, according to the Met Office. An official heatwave is declared when temperatures rise above the heatwave threshold for three consecutive days. The threshold varies from 25C to 28C across different counties.

SpaceX Starship V3 launch live: How to watch 'most powerful rocket ever' blast off

The countdown has started ahead of the launch of the most powerful SpaceX rocket ever built that may one day take humans to Mars.

News.content:
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered the country's near-weapons-grade uranium is not sent abroad - but Donald Trump has threatened to hit Iran 'even harder' if Tehran does not agree to his demands

Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has ordered Iran's near-weapons-grade uranium stay in the country, according to two senior Iranian sources - a move expected to further anger Donald Trump.

The US President has threatened to hit Iran "even harder" and get a "little bit nasty" if a peace deal is not reached soon - with all US demands so far aimed at preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

"We hit them very hard. We may have to hit them even harder - but maybe not," Trump said during an address at the US Coast Guard Academy yesterday. "But we're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon and blow up the entire Middle East, Israel, the entire Middle East, and then come here for you. Not going to happen."

Benjamin Netanyahu has said he will not consider the war over until enriched uranium is removed from Iran.

Officers injured as police car 'rammed at speed' in Northern Ireland

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) says two officers were injured when the car they were travelling in was rammed by another vehicle in Co Down

View Image Two police officers were injured (stock) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Police have launched an appeal after two officers travelling in a car were rammed by another vehicle in Co Down, Northern Ireland.

‌



Tactical Support Group officers from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) were conducting a mobile patrol on the Killysorrell Road, near Blackskull, at around 12.15pm on Wednesday afternoon when they encountered a beige/gold coloured Ford Galaxy with defective number plates.

‌



The officers, who were travelling in an unmarked Skoda, followed the car a short distance to Villa Wood Road where it stopped suddenly and reversed into the police vehicle, Belfast Live reports.

‌



The Ford Galaxy continued on to the Gowdystown Road, where it once again stopped and reversed at speed into the police car before making off southbound on the A1 carriageway.

Two officers required medical treatment following the incident, and the police vehicle sustained frontal damage, causing it to be off the road for a period for repairs.

News.title: Teacher denies murdering and sexually abusing baby but says he is 'ashamed'
News.content:
Teacher denies murdering and sexually abusing baby but says he is 'ashamed'

Jamie Varley, 37, and John McGowan-Fazakerly, 32, face a string of charges following baby Preston's death in July 2023

View 4 Images 13-month-old Preston Dave (Image: Lancashire Police/PA Wire)

A teacher accused of the murder of an adopted baby told a jury he never hurt or sexually abused the child.

‌



Jamie Varley, 37, became emotional at times during his evidence from the witness box as he denied the murder of 13-month-old Preston Davey. He denied taking photos or videos as “trophies” of sexual abuse but said he felt “disappointed” and “really ashamed” at some images he had taken on his phone.

‌



Varley is alleged to have routinely sexually, physically and emotionally abused the baby he had adopted with his partner John McGowan-Fazakerley, 32, Preston Crown Court has heard. Both men deny all charges.

‌



In the fourth week of the trial, Varley gave evidence in his own defence for the first time, his voice sometimes breaking with emotion as videos and photos of the baby were shown on screens in the courtroom.

View 4 Images Jamie Varley is accused of murder (Image: X)

Nick Johnson KC, defending Varley, began his questions by asking him: “On the 27th of July 2023, did you kill Preston Davey by deliberately blocking his airway?"

‌



“No, I did not,” Varley replied. Mr Johnson continued: “Did you sexually assault that child in any way?... Did you ever wilfully harm Preston physically or psychologically?”

Varley replied: “Absolutely not, our son has never been sexually abused. No.” Jurors heard, after undergoing an assessment and familiarisation process, Preston was adopted and began living with the defendants at their home in Blackpool on April 1 2023.

But it is alleged in the next four months before his death he was routinely ill-treated, had indecent images and videos taken of him, and was sexually abused and physically assaulted, suffering 40 traumatic injuries found at post mortem.

‌



View 4 Images Preston died in 2023

The court heard Varley, who said he has severe dyslexia, became a design and technology teacher and head of year at a local high school before meeting his partner. He said: “I had always thought about having kids, I wanted to be a teacher, a daddy, just never thought it was possible once I realised I was a gay man.

“John was everything I had ever asked for in a relationship... My whole life just changed when I met John.”

‌



Varley said the “early stages” of adoption was an “eye opener” and that Preston was not a good sleeper or in a routine. He added: “It was challenging in the sense it was new to us.

“I felt because I had more experience than John, I felt it was going to be a breeze, but it wasn’t.”

Varley was asked to explain a text he sent to his sister about Preston, saying: “He’s dead meat” after a sleepless night. Varley said: “It was just language that I use. In social settings I’m dramatic. Sassy. I just easily throw words about.”

‌



View 4 Images John McGowan-Fazakerley (Image: LancsLive/MEN)

The defendant told jurors he had bonded with the baby better than he expected, as he did not think he could love anything more than his dog, Max, but his love for Preston exceeded that for his pet. He added: “When we got the little one, it was special, it was quick, it was strong.”

Mr Johnson then asked Varley about photos of bruises on Preston, who appeared to have a “cluster” of bruises on his forehead, which child sex abuse expert, Dr Joanne Gifford, had described as a “red flag” for signs of abuse.

‌



Varley said the baby, who was learning to crawl, would often bang his head and daily have little mishaps but denied ever deliberately bruising the child.

Mr Johnson asked about a photo of Preston playing naked in a paddling pool which Home Office pathologist Dr Alison Armour said showed a shaded mark on the child’s bottom which resembled a human bite mark.

Mr Johnson said: “Did you ever bite Preston’s bottom?... What do you say to the suggestion you bit him and took a photo?”

‌



Varley replied: “Absolutely not... Could not be more wrong.”

Mr Johnson asked Varley about a series of photos on Varley’s phone of Preston in his cot, along with two toy teddy bears, four days before his death in July 2023. The images stretch over a period of three minutes and 12 seconds, with the child’s head and arms over the top horizontal bar of his cot and his neck resting on the bar.

His body is apparently partially suspended, his legs in a “frog like” position and the child seemingly asleep or unconscious, described to the jury earlier as a “very unsafe” and “dangerous” position.

‌



Varley said the baby had gone to sleep before in “funny positions” and had done so again so he took photos. Mr Johnson said: “Were these trophies of a sexual encounter?”

“No they were not, no,” Varley replied. He added: “I did not even recognise at the moment, it was inappropriate.

“I’m disappointed. I feel shamed. I feel really ashamed.

‌



“I did not mean to cause any distress, any harm in that moment, I felt he was safe.

“I just wanted to capture him, all of his life.

“I just wanted to capture every part of his life.”

‌



Four days later Preston was rushed to hospital on July 27 2023, having suffered a collapse and cardiac arrest, allegedly following a sexual assault by Varley.

Varley told police he had briefly left the child in the bath and when he returned he was off his bath seat and submerged. But a post-mortem examination ruled out drowning and found multiple non-accidental, internal and external injuries.

Preston’s cause of death was found to be acute upper airways obstruction by either smothering or an object or objects inserted into his mouth. The jury has heard some injuries to Preston were possibly caused by “forcible penetration” and parts of his anatomy “abnormal” with his injuries clinical signs of sexual abuse.

Article continues below

Varley denies murder, manslaughter, two counts of assault by penetration, five counts of cruelty to a child, grievous bodily harm, sexual assault of a child, 13 counts of taking indecent photos or videos of a child, one of distributing an indecent photo of a child, to his co-accused, and one of making an indecent photo.

McGowan-Fazakerley denies allowing the death of a child, three counts of child cruelty and one count of the sexual assault of a child.

The trial was adjourned until Friday morning.

News.title: Ebola hospital at centre of outbreak set on fire by angry mob
News.content:
Ebola hospital at centre of outbreak set on fire by angry mob

An angry crowd set fire to a field hospital set up to treat Ebola patients at the centre of the outbreak after nurses refused to let them see the body of a man who died of the disease

View 4 Images Angry scenes erupted at an Ebola field hospital in DR Congo (Image: AP Photo/Dirole Lotsima Dieudonn)

An emergency Ebola treatment centre responding to a major outbreak has been set on fire by an angry mob.

‌



The incident unfolded in a town in the eastern Congo today after the crowd were stopped from retrieving the body of a local man, local police said.

‌



It comes as the number of people who have died in the Central Africa Ebola outbreak rose to 139, with more than 600 suspected cases.

‌



Experts from the World Health Organisation warned yesterday that it could take as long as nine months before a vaccine against Bundibugyo, the specific form of Ebola behind the spate of infections, is ready.

View 4 Images Security guards were rushed out to bring the situation under control (Image: AP Photo/Dirole Lotsima Dieudonn)

The centre in Rwampara was burnt by local youths who were stopped from retrieving the body of a friend said to have died of Ebola, one eyewitness said.

‌



They told the Associated Press: "The police intervened to try to calm the situation, but unfortunately they were unsuccessful. The young people ended up setting fire to the centre. That's the situation." An AP journalist saw people break into the centre and set fire to objects inside and also to what appeared to be the body of at least one suspected Ebola victim that was being stored there. Aid workers fled the treatment centre in vehicles.

View 4 Images Medical staff moved in to disinfect the site after the fire was extinguished (Image: AP Photo/Moses Sawasawa)

Deputy Senior Commissioner Jean Claude Mukendi, head of the public security department in Ituri Province, said there had been confusion in the crowd about the procedures burying suspected Ebola victims. He told reporters: "His family, friends, and other young people wanted to take his body home for a funeral even though the instructions from the authorities during this Ebola virus outbreak are clear. All bodies must be buried according to the regulations."

‌



View 4 Images The fire was started by a group of local youths after they were stopped from seeing the body of an Ebola victim pal (Image: AP Photo/Dirole Lotsima Dieudonn)

Hama Amadou, the field Coordinator for the humanitarian organisation ALIMA, which was working at the site, said later that calm had been restored and the aid teams were continuing their work at the centre.

It comes as Congolese authorities and multiple international aid agencies desperately attempt to contain the outbreak, which has been designated as a "global health emergency" by the WHO.

Article continues below

The Democratic Republic of Congo national football team has cancelled its pre-World Cup training camp in the capital, Kinshasa, because of the outbreak. They are due to play friendly matches against Denmark on June 3, and Chile on June 9.

News.title: Trump's team claim to have built Ebola treatment centres in Uganda - but nobody there is aware of them
News.content:
Trump's team claim to have built Ebola treatment centres in Uganda - but nobody there is aware of them

A statement from Donald Trump's White House claiming they had set up treatment centres in 'Ebola-affected' areas of Uganda has been denied by the country's health ministry

View 3 Images Donald Trump's White House has been rebuffed for claiming it had set up Ebola 'treatment centres' (Image: Getty Images)

The Ugandan government has said they are 'not aware' of any new Ebola treatment centres in their country after Donald Trump's White House claimed to have set them up.

‌



In a statement earlier this week, the US Department of State announced it was "funding up to 50 treatment clinics" in "Ebola-affected regions of the DRC and Uganda" amid the current outbreak in Central Africa, which has left 131 dead and more than 530 infected.

‌



But last night, the Ugandan ministry of health denied that any treatment centres had been set up and insisted the "country remains safe", with the two recorded fatalities being patients "imported" from the DR Congo.

‌



World Cup nation issues statement after cancelling training camp amid Ebola fears READ MORE :

View 3 Images Workers line up to disinfect their protective equipment at General Referral Hospital of Mongbwalu (Image: Getty Images)

They wrote on X (formerly Twitter): "The Ministry of Health has not been engaged on the establishment of the treatment centres referred to here, and we are therefore not aware of where they may have been set up within the country.

"We continue to affirm that Uganda has so far registered only two imported Ebola cases: one fatality and one patient currently responding well to treatment under close medical care. There are no local infections and the country remains safe."

‌



It comes as questions build over whether the initial statement - which lauded $23 million in "bilateral foreign assistance" for both DR Congo and Uganda - was fully fact-checked.

The update on Tuesday added: "Today, the United States announced a broad commitment to rapidly support the response by funding up to 50 treatment clinics, and associated frontline costs being established in Ebola-affected regions of the DRC and Uganda.

"These rapidly deployed clinics will enable implementing partners to establish clinical care and containment perimetres around affected areas. Clinics will provide."

‌



View 3 Images Checks are being carried out at the border between Uganda and the DR Congo (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Trump's White House has meanwhile banned anyone who has recently travelled to either country from entering the US - unless they land at Washington Dulles International Airport subject themselves to "enhanced screening".

On Thursday, US Customs and Border Protection said an Air France flight bound for Detroit was diverted to Montreal after a passenger from the Congo boarded a flight in Paris "in error" due to the flight restrictions.

Article continues below

A spokesperson for the agency says the passenger “should not have boarded” the plane on Wednesday due to U.S. entry restrictions put in place to reduce the risk of Ebola spreading.

The spokesman said in an email officials “took decisive action and prohibited the flight carrying that traveler from landing at Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport, and instead, diverted to Montreal, Canada.”

Air France said the Congolese passenger was denied entry into the U.S. due to new regulations that travelers from certain countries, including the Congo, can enter only through Washington DC.

Aston Villa striker Ollie Watkins is set to be included - after helping his side win the Europa League on Wednesday - alongside Al-Ahli striker Ivan Toney, who has scored 32 goals in 32 games in the Saudi Arabian league this season.

Nottingham Forest midfielder Morgan Gibbs-White is set to miss out, despite being the top-scoring English player in the Premier League this season, alongside Watkins and Dominic Calvert-Lewin, on 14 goals.

Fresh off multiple Trump critics losing in the Republican primaries, the president is reportedly drawing his next GOP target list for the 2028 elections.

It could include Rep. Lauren Boebert, who clashed with the president over releasing the Epstein files, and Sen. Rand Paul, who has challenged the president’s unilateral war effort in Iran, Axios reports.

Over the weekend, President Trump openly called for someone to challenge the Colorado congresswoman, who angered the president by campaigning for Rep. Thomas Massie, a rare GOP critic of Trump in the House and another key leader in the Epstein files push.

“Is anyone interested in running against Weak Minded Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s Fourth Congressional District?” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Saturday.

“I knew the risks when I agreed to stand by my friend Thomas Massie,” Boebert wrote on X in response, adding that she was not “mad or offended.”

open image in gallery The president hasn’t been afraid to endorse challengers against GOP politicians this cycle, and he’s reportedly drawing up his hit list for 2028 ( Reuters )

“I was, and will be, America First, America Always, and MAGA.”

The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

Trump’s allies have been clear that critics of the president could face the Republican’s wrath down the line, even though he’s terming out in 2028.

“Do not ever doubt President Trump and his political power,” White House communications director Steven Cheung wrote on X on Tuesday, as Massie and fellow part-time Trump critic Sen. Bill Cassidy lost in their primaries. “F*** around, find out.”

Even Republican stalwarts can quickly find themselves on the outs with Trump — just ask former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, who resigned in January after a brutal public feud with the president — but the president’s revenge tour has its downsides.

open image in gallery Trump has called for a primary challenger against Rep. Laurent Boebert, who was a key figure in the push to release the Epstein files ( Getty )

The Republican Party only has a three-vote edge in the Senate, and President Trump may have imperiled that this election season thanks to Cassidy’s impending exit, the president’s decision to endorse a challenger to GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, and the increasingly emboldened Sen. Thom Tillis, who is retiring after repeated clashes with Trump.

Looking forward, the most brutal 2028 contest in the party is likely for the presidential nomination.

Unless Trump indulges his fantasy of running for an illegal third term, a 2028 presidential primary will likely pit Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio against each other, and Trump seems to enjoy openly speculating about which of his successors will claim the spot.

Whatever happens in 2028, Democrats remain projected to retake the House this year, given the usual mid-administration decline in seats, plus Trump’s increasingly unpopular status and voter anger over rising prices and the war with Iran.

Noah Wyle is standing up for healthcare workers after decades of highlighting their industry’s challenges in his portrayals of fictional doctors.

The Emmy-winning star of The Pitt joined his mother, a retired orthopedic and operating room nurse, and a crowd of healthcare professionals and bipartisan lawmakers Thursday at a rally on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. to advocate for policies to better support the medical workforce.

“This isn’t about politics,” Wyle, 54, said at the Health Care Workers Rally. “Cancer is not partisan. A stroke is not partisan. A kid with a fever in the middle of night is not partisan. The healthcare professional who shows up for that patient should not have to beg for basic support from a system that they hold together.”

Following a line-up of nurses and doctors who spoke at the event, Wyle was visibly emotional as he took the stage directly after his mother, Marjorie Speer, and greeted her with a hug. He opened: “Following my mother is a tough act anywhere. Following her at a rally for healthcare professionals at the United States Capitol is a different kind of impossible.”

The actor continued: “I want to be super clear about who is talking to you right now: I am not a doctor. I am not a nurse. I am not a member in any way of the healthcare workforce that I love so dearly. I am an actor. I’m the son of a nurse who spent 50 years caring for other people, and I’ve spent decades trying to do justice to what she, and the rest of you, actually do. That is the only credential I am claiming today.”

open image in gallery Noah Wyle plays Dr. Robby on ‘The Pitt’ ( HBO )

open image in gallery Noah Wyle led a rally in Washington, DC, advocating for healthcare workers alongside his mother ( AFP/Getty )

The rally was aimed at pressuring lawmakers to fund a trio of bills to support healthcare workers: the Healthcare of Human Act, which would provide federal tax credits for medical professionals working in short-staffed areas; the Dr. Lorna Breen Healthcare Provider Protection Act, which would fund programs focused on mental health and well-being; and the Healthcare Professionals Speak Free Act, which would protect workers who speak up about workplace safety from retaliation.

Wyle, who plays Dr. Michael “Robby” Robinavitch on the popular HBO Max medical drama, got his start by playing another emergency medicine doctor, Dr. John Carter, on the NBC medical drama ER for 11 seasons.

He has spoken in the past about being inspired by stories from actual medical professionals to accurately represent the pressures of the healthcare industry in media.

“What I learned from this show, and what is now in my bones, is that medicine is hard enough, but so much of the damage is coming from everything around medicine,” Wyle said during the rally.

He concluded: “To every healthcare professional here, and every healthcare professional watching, I know you do not need another speech about how important you are. You need back up.”

Getting a scalp or face massage is often a relaxing highlight of getting a haircut or a facial. Now, head spas are popping up across the country offering deep cranial and facial relaxation.

“Typically, when you go get a massage, the focus is always like your back, and I always wish there was more on my head, on my face especially, on my neck,” says Karena Kong, a frequent customer of Nen Head Spa in San Francisco. “When I saw that they give 90 minutes of just head, face, shoulder massage, I felt like it’s a great way to just focus on the areas that I love.”

What to expect from a head spa

Head spas originated in Japan, rooted in centuries-old practices that combine massage and herbal tinctures. Modern versions began gaining popularity in Japanese salons in the 1990s before spreading throughout Asia and now the U.S.

A typical session lasts 60 or 90 minutes and often begins with a scalp inspection, followed by deep cleansing, exfoliation, steam, and extended head, face and neck massage. Many services also include essential oils, conditioning masks, and aromatherapy in a quiet setting with dimmed lights and soft music.

“The core part of it is actually getting your hair washed,” said Peter Tham, owner of Nen Head Spa, where head massages cost about $100 an hour. “The feeling of getting your head washed, especially on a hot and humid day, feels really good. Combine that with, facial, scalp, neck and shoulder massages, which is kind of where most people, especially those who sit in front of a computer all day, suffer a lot of tension.”

What to make of head spa claims

Some head spas make health and medical claims about some of their services, suggesting they can offer stress relief or treatment for scalp skin conditions, hair loss or even alopecia, an autoimmune disorder. Experts caution that people with skin or hair conditions should see a dermatologist or other appropriate doctor for advice and possible treatment.

“It’s important to know and differentiate something that’s done for a health reason or relaxation from seeing a medical expert, a dermatologist, if you are having hair loss,” said Zakia Rahman, a dermatology professor at Stanford University School of Medicine.

Rahman has noticed the rising popularity of head spas and says they are generally fine as a compliment to actual medical treatments if needed — and for people who like the way it makes them feel.

Head spas can be relaxing and rejuvenating, fans say

At Sunday Headspa in San Francisco, each session starts with a technician inspecting hair follicles with a magnifying device and assessing their condition. Then customers get a deep clean, said Jolly Mac, the spa’s coordinator.

Many of their clients first discovered head spa services in Asia and are looking for similar services, which start at about $200 an hour.

Customer Crystle Vitari, first visited a head spa while visiting South Korea and finds it “rejuvenating” — and relaxing.

“Every time, I fall asleep and take a nap, actually, because it’s so relaxing," she said.

___

Associated Press writer Olga R. Rodriguez contributed to this story.

A college graduate had both of her legs violently ripped off by a boat propeller after she drunkenly jumped overboard at the encouragement of the tour boat’s staff, a lawsuit claims.

Hannah Smith, 22, claims she was plied with rum punch cocktails spiked with sedatives by bar staff on a Catamaran Ferry taking her on a day trip to Pearl Island Beach during a Carnival cruise last May.

Smith, who was celebrating graduating summa cum laude from Alabama’s Miles College with a friend, asked the boat staff where the restroom was, and was told, “The ocean is your toilet,” prompting her to jump into the water to relieve herself.

But as she entered the water, the ferry captain started the boat’s engine, causing Smith to be “violently and forcibly grabbed, sucked underwater and brutally slashed,” according to a federal complaint obtained by the Daily Mail.

Her left leg was immediately amputated by the propeller, but she managed to escape using her right leg and because her friend, Brooklyn Pitre, 22, helped pull her up, the suit claims.

open image in gallery A college graduate lost both of her legs in an accident after jumping off a boat in the Bahamas, according to a lawsuit ( GoFundMe )

“When [she] was pulled out of the water, her left leg below her knee was almost completely severed from her body except for a sliver of skin, and she had suffered multiple gashes throughout both legs and pelvis area,” the lawsuit said.

“The injuries caused [her] to lose over 60 percent of all her blood — by itself life-threatening.”

Smith was rushed to a hospital in Nassau before being flown to a hospital in Miami in critical condition. She was given 20 units of blood and underwent 25 surgeries, including the amputation of her right leg below the knee, before she was discharged two months later.

The college grad blames the staff on the excursion trip for “grooming” her and her friends and loading them up with complimentary 16-ounce cups of rum punch, according to the lawsuit.

During the booze-filled trip, a bartender poured a potent mixed drink spiked with a sedating substance directly into Smith’s mouth, while another worker on the boat encouraged Smith and her friend to puff on a marijuana joint.

According to her lawsuit, Smith’s blood alcohol level reached 0.447 — four times what is considered legally impaired in Florida.

open image in gallery Smith lost 60 percent of her blood in the accident, according to the lawsuit ( GoFundMe )

Smith is suing the tour group, Pearl Investment Management Group, and boat operator, Sun Cay, for negligence.

Carnival Cruise is also named in the lawsuit, as Smith’s lawyers argue that the cruise line marketed the day trip as a vetted, safe outing for passengers.

A spokesperson for Carnival told Daily Mail: “Our thoughts are with Ms. Smith, and we wish her strength and healing.”

“At Carnival Cruise Line, we continuously strive to keep our guests and crew safe as a priority. Out of respect for ongoing legal proceedings, we are unable to comment further.”

“We remain committed to supporting safety and well-being in all we do.”

The Independent has contacted Carnival for more information.

News.title: Kyle Busch to miss NASCAR race this weekend due to hospitalization
News.content:
Two-time NASCAR Cup Series champion Kyle Busch has been hospitalized with a severe illness and will not compete in the Coca-Cola 600 at Charlotte Motor Speedway this weekend.

His family announced the news on social media, requesting privacy during his treatment, and Austin Hill is set to replace him in the No. 8 Chevrolet.

This marks the first time in over a decade that Busch has been absent from a Cup Series race, with his last significant absence occurring in 2015 due to injuries.

Richard Childress Racing, Busch's team, released a statement affirming their full support for his health and wishing him a safe and speedy recovery.

Busch, a formidable figure in NASCAR with 234 career wins, is currently ranked 24th in the Cup Series standings this season.

Social media companies including Meta have settled the first of many lawsuits brought by hundreds of school districts seeking compensation for costs they say they incurred dealing with harms to children's mental health from social media addiction.

The lawsuit brought by a small, rural Kentucky school district was set to go to trial next month in federal court in Oakland, California. The judge and the parties selected it as a bellwether case — essentially a test for both sides to see how their arguments play out before a jury — out of 1,200 similar cases. The settlement only applies to the Breathitt County School District.

Meta reached a settlement with the district Thursday, following settlements earlier this week with the other defendants in the case — TikTok, Snap and Google’s YouTube.

The financial terms of the settlements were not disclosed. The school district had sought more than $60 million to create a 15-year program it said would help counteract mental health and learning issues caused by social media.

The plaintiffs’ attorneys said in a statement that their "focus remains on pursuing justice for the remaining 1,200 school districts who have filed cases.”

The settlement follows court losses earlier this year for Meta and YouTube in social media harms lawsuits in California and New Mexico.

In March, Meta and YouTube were found liable for designing addictive features following a trial in Los Angeles. The plaintiff, known by her initials KGM, claimed she became addicted to social media as a child and that it exacerbated her mental health struggles. A jury sided with her and awarded about $6 million in damages.

And in New Mexico, a jury determined that Meta harms children’s mental health and safety, in violation of state law.

News.title: Protesters storm Ebola hospital to retrieve victim’s body
News.content:
Protesters have stormed an Ebola treatment centre in the Democratic Republic of Congo to retrieve the body of a relative, according to local media reports.

Footage circulating online appeared to show parts of Rwampara Hospital engulfed in flames, with plumes of smoke rising above the facility. Gunshots can be heard in the background.

“Angry protesters are setting fire to the tents housing Ebola patients because they want to forcibly retrieve the bodies,” said one man, his face mask pulled below his mouth.

Health authorities oversee the burials of suspected victims in line with strict infection protocols, but this often brings them into conflict with grieving families who want to perform traditional burial rites for their loved ones.

Similar incidents have been a feature of previous Ebola outbreaks, particularly families digging up the bodies of deceased relatives for re-burial – an extremely dangerous act because corpses remain highly contagious for up to a week after death.

In 2022, a cluster of Ebola cases in Uganda was traced back to a family who exhumed their relative at night, undoing the work of a safe burial team in order to give the deceased man a funeral. Within days, at least 23 of the mourners had contracted Ebola and three were dead.

The unrest in Rwampara reportedly erupted on Thursday after the death of a young man suspected of having Ebola at the hospital, which is located around 7.5 miles from Bunia, the capital of the conflict-wracked eastern Ituri province.

News.title: Scientists to monitor British cruise passengers in hantavirus study
News.content:
British passengers repatriated from the cruise ship hit by an outbreak of hantavirus will be monitored for signs of infection as part of a long-term study.

More than 20 Britons who were potentially exposed to the disease on board the MV Hondius have volunteered for the study, which is being run by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the University of Liverpool, the Pandemic Sciences Institute at the University of Oxford, the University of Edinburgh and the University of Glasgow.

It aims to generate robust research on the Andes strain of hantavirus, which is the only variant of the disease known to spread between people but is poorly understood and has no approved vaccine.

After they stop isolating, the volunteers will continue to provide blood samples for testing at Porton Down, the government research facility tasked with studying dangerous pathogens like Ebola, anthrax, and plague.

None of the British passengers who have returned to the UK have so far tested positive for hantavirus. But due to the virus’s long incubation period, which can be up to two months, it is possible they could still become unwell or be asymptomatic carriers of the disease.

One study has previously found that hantavirus could remain in human semen for up to six years and has the potential for sexual transmission, even after a person has recovered.

If a male patient tests positive for the virus, investigators will also look to test their semen for ongoing signs of infection.

“If we do have a case, we can study that in more detail and think about the mechanisms of the disease and how we can treat that disease better,” said Professor Lance Turtle, Chair in Immunity and Infectious Diseases at the University of Liverpool and Joint Chief Investigator in the study.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo wins first Al Nassr trophy after three years in Saudi Arabia as footie legend, 41, nets rare free kick
Sports.content:
CRISTIANO RONALDO has finally ended his three-year wait for a trophy at Al-Nassr.

The Portuguese icon was on hand in the club’s 4-1 win over Damac at the Alawwal Park in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.





The win and the three points confirmed Al-Nassr‘s place as champions of the Saudi Pro League.

Ronaldo, 41, and co headed into the match needing at least a point to hold off rivals Al-Hilal.

Former Liverpool star Sadio Mane opened the scoring in the 31st minute before Kinsley Coman doubled the lead after the break.

Morlaye Sylla nabbed one back for Damac before Ronaldo stepped up to put the result beyond doubt.

The five-time Ballon d’Or winner netted in the 62nd and 80th minutes to give Al-Nassr a three-goal cushion.

His first goal was the pick of the bunch as he managed to score a rare free-kick from a tight angle.

Despite his prolific form since making the move to Saudi Arabia, trophies had evaded the serial winner.

But after three years of trying, Ronaldo can finally call himself champion again.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Ronaldo will be able to add the league title to his collection and take his record to being champion of four different top-flight leagues.

He did not finish the match as he was subbed off in the closing stages by manager Jorge Jesus.

As the full-time whistle closed in, Ronaldo could be seen to break down into tears as Al-Nassr closed in on glory.

He made the switch to Saudi Arabia after falling out with former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag.



The forward signed a stunning, big-money contract worth £178million-a year.

He had kept up his performances on the pitch despite his advancing years.

Ronaldo has scored 123 goals for Al-Nassr in 142 games, just 18 short of his total tally for United.



He had managed the staggering number in 204 appearances fewer as well.

This season, he has scored 28 goals in 30 league appearances but will not take home the Golden Boot.

That honour will go to former Brentford striker Ivan Toney, who hit 32 goals in 32 appearances for Al-Ahli.

Ronaldo has suffered some issues at Al-Nassr this season as he missed a couple of games in February.

He was furious with the club’s owners for not investing enough in the playing staff and believed their rivals would surpass them.

Ronaldo will now be hoping to continue his club success on to the international stage with the World Cup this summer.

The veteran was called up to Portugal’s squad for the tournament across Canada, Mexico and the USA.

The Tottenham star suffered the injury in the closing stages of Tuesday’s 2-1 defeat to Chelsea.





Spence, 25, was hurt in a tussle with striker Liam Delap as he took an elbow to the face.

The Blues ace was penalised for the foul, but the full-back is still paying the price.

Spence went for medical checks after the match and it was discovered that he had in fact broken his jaw in the challenge.

The World Cup hopeful will feature in the match with the help of a protective face mask.

The news of Spence’s mangled mandible comes just a day before Thomas Tuchel‘s squad for this summer‘s World Cup is announced.

Spence has an outside shot of being included in the final 26.

He has only made four appearances for the Three Lions – all of which have come under Tuchel.

Sports.title: Celtic vs Hearts referee ‘ended match without blowing whistle’ as Scottish FA reveal little-known rule
Sports.content:
CELTIC’S controversial title-clinching victory over Hearts was brought to a bizarre end without the referee ever blowing the final whistle.

The Hoops ran out 3-1 winners to miraculously land their 56th Scottish league title — but the historic achievement was instantly overshadowed by total pandemonium.





Chaos erupted at Celtic Park when thousands of jubilant fans stormed the pitch after Callum Osmand netted a dramatic third goal in the 97th minute.

Despite there being around 30 seconds left on the clock, referee Don Robertson never restarted the action as the turf vanished under a sea of green and white.

In the terrifying aftermath, Hearts claimed there were reports that some of their players had been assaulted on the pitch.

The Edinburgh club slammed the “menacing and threatening” scenes before the Jambos were rushed out of the stadium straight onto the team bus for their own safety.

Hearts chiefs released a blistering statement questioning why the game was halted by a security breach rather than a whistle from the match officials.

While some fans insisted Hearts should actually have been awarded the three points – and the league title that would have come with them – with the game abandoned due to the fan invasion.

But SPFL bosses have fired back, insisting the match was correctly ended.

The Scottish FA have now released the official VAR audio, which proves Robertson called time AFTER the full eight minutes of injury time had been played.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Sensationally, the audio also revealed that Hearts manager Derek McInnes had actually begged officials to stop the game due to major safety concerns for his players.

The referee complied, bringing the curtain down on the match despite never actually placing the whistle to his lips.

The dramatic move is fully protected by a little-known IFAB rule which gives referees power over the match clock.

A statement from the Scottish FA read: “In the interests of transparency, we are happy to set out the facts.



“Regarding references to a ‘premature ending of the match’, the Scottish FA’s Chief Governance Officer, Gary Booth, the Head of Refereeing, William Collum, and VAR Manager Martin Atkinson reviewed the audio-visual footage of the period in question on Monday at the club’s request, with Mr Paterson in attendance.

“While it was the agreed intention for this meeting to be conducted privately, recent statements have compelled us to consider the public interest in providing clarification and chronology.

“It was made clear at that meeting that the match official, Don Robertson, took the correct action in ending the game.

“We note there has been speculation regarding the blowing of a final whistle.



“The Laws of the Game require the referee to signal the end of the match, but do not prescribe the method of that signal.

“In the context of what unfolded – which is verified by the footage and the Match Incident Report submitted to the Scottish FA – the match official clearly communicated that the match was ended and not abandoned.

“In addition, the match clock does not stop when a goal is scored.

“The footage shows that when the match official confirms the game has ended, the clock is at 53.07 [98.07], more than the minimum additional time of eight minutes signalled.



“It was also apparent from the audio that this decision was taken following dialogue with the Hearts Head Coach, who had intimated concerns over player safety.

“For the avoidance of doubt, Law 5 of the IFAB Laws of the Game state that ‘the decisions of the referee regarding facts connected with play are final’.
