World.title: Half Australia's farms are in trusts. So what does tax reform mean for farmers?
World.content:
Half Australian farms are held in family trusts, so how will farmers be affected by the federal tax overhaul?

Farmers use trusts to protect their assets, distribute income within their families and ensure the farm can be passed on to the next generation without incurring a large tax bill.

The importance of trusts in managing farm finances has led the federal government to provide an exemption for primary producer income from the new minimum 30 per cent tax on trust income.

But the tax reforms could still have dramatic implications for farmers when they sell their farms.

So, what do the changes mean for farmers and why are they worried?

Why do farmers use trusts?

There are around 40,000 trusts with primary producer income in Australia.

Those trusts allow income to be distributed strategically within farming families to lower the overall taxable income.

Loading

The National Farmers Federation (NFF) was deeply concerned about the potential impact of a flat 30 per cent tax on trusts.

CEO Mike Guerin said securing a carve-out for primary production income was vital.

Without it, he said the policy could have "destroyed agriculture in its current form as a family-owned enterprise within a generation".

Farming income has been excluded from the 30 per cent minimum tax on family trusts. (Landline: Andrew Chounding )

But farmers will still be impacted by the tax changes.

A change to the way properties bought before 1985 are taxed could see farmers paying a much higher rate into the future.

Many modern farms have also diversified their business beyond what they harvest from the land.

Income from farm stays, wineries, renewable energy projects, livestock transport and other agronomy businesses will all now be taxed at a minimum 30 per cent.

And retired farmers who leased farmland back to children or neighbours through family trust structures will also be subject to the new tax rules.

Succession planning

One of the main reasons farmers use discretionary trusts is to ensure their main asset, the farm itself, is protected from lawsuits, bankruptcy, death and divorce.

Tony Flanery is a farmer with his own discretionary trust and he said the structure is important.

"A divorce could mean, for want of a better word, an attack on the assets of the family farm and a discretionary trust has the ability to operate without the divorce or a death destroying the business," he said.

He said it was also critical for succession planning.

"You might have four different properties that are owned by a trust and they're all different sizes, so there's the ability to allocate which property might go to which family member," he said.

Control of the trust can be transferred from a farmer to their child without triggering capital gains tax.

However, when the assets are transferred outside the trust structure, when a farmer sells a property to fund their retirement or pay out a non-farming family member, the farmer needs to pay capital gains tax (CGT).

What happens when the farm is sold?

Many Australian farms are held in family trusts for generations.

Under the old rules if a farm was purchased before CGT was introduced in 1985, when it's sold the seller doesn't have to pay tax on the gain.

Loading

The recent changes mean that future gains on the asset will now be subject to CGT.

From July 1, 2027, the existing 50 per cent CGT discount for all assets held longer than 12 months will be replaced with inflation-adjusted indexation, and a minimum 30 per cent tax on capital gains.

Owners will be required to value pre-1985 assets on June 30, 2027 and any capital gain accrued from that point will become taxable when they sell.

Georgiena Ryan, commercial and property lawyer, thinks farmers will be taxed at a higher rate under the new rules announced in the budget. (Supplied)

Georgiena Ryan, a commercial and property lawyer with 40 years' experience advising clients on tax, agribusiness and water law, lives on a farm and has compared the tax that would be paid on a typical rural property in her area under the new regime against the previous rules.

While the laws won't apply retrospectively, she said it is possible that farmers could end up paying a lot more tax in the future.

She said 1,000 acres bought in 2003 for $500/acre ($500,000) would now be worth $5,600 an acre or $5,600,000, based on the most recent valuer general valuations.

Farms which have been passed down for generations may now be subject to tax when they are sold. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

"If we allow $100 per acre for duty, costs and money spent over the years, giving a cost base of $600/acre ($600,000), then under the current system the gain would be $5,000 an acre ($5,000,000)," she said.

"Applying the 50 per cent discount, the taxable gain is $2,500,000.

"Leaving aside any other income, I would pay tax on that of $1,091,138."

She then applied the new rules which use the consumer price index (CPI) to calculate capital gain on the same property — $600/acre ($600,000) from 2003 (CPI 78.6) to 2025 (140.6).

When sold the cost base of the property would be $1,076 per acre ($1,076,000) so the taxable gain would be $4,524,000.

"Leaving aside any other income, I would pay tax on that of $2,001,938" — an extra $910,800 in tax."

Farmers delay transferring farms to next generation

Farmer and accountant Peter Knights is concerned that some families are holding onto properties when it would be better to pass them on.

There are tax provisions in place that apply to farm sales.

If the farm's turnover is less than $2 million or the net asset value is under $6 million then it will qualify for small business concessions.

A Treasury spokesperson said this means eligible farmers can pay reduced or no capital gains tax at all when they sell.

However the $6 million asset limit has not increased for almost two decades in which time the value of farmland has increased dramatically, meaning many farms no longer qualify.

Farmer and accountant Peter Knights said this situation has led to some families holding onto properties when it might be better to pass them on.

"We're finding more and more that our clients are outside those thresholds when the time is right to make a transfer of assets to the next generation … so people hang onto it for too long."

" So the people who have the appetite to produce don't get the asset. "

NFF president Hamish McIntyre says the carve-out for agriculture is a big win, but there are still concerns for family trusts. (National Farmers Federation)

Are the proposed changes fair?

Shumi Akhtar, associate professor at the University of Sydney Business School said the federal government should be cautious about changes that affect the farm sector.

But she said the government is trying to close tax loopholes.

"Some people may exploit a loophole, it could be international investors pretending to invest in a farm, [and] they are trying to close that," she said,

"Government is not going after genuine, innocent farmers, they are trying to hold the bad actors accountable."

She also said there is a long way to go before the changes are finalised.

"No clear-cut rules or legislation has been released yet … farmers need to wait until the detailed legislation is released."

Farmers are talking to their accountants about the raft of changes.

President of the NFF Hamish McIntyre warned that agriculture is different to other parts of the economy and these changes could threaten productivity.

"It's more that transfer when the time comes for the next generation when we think it will be tricky," he said.

"We learn to farm by watching our own parents, and then we pass it our children."

For productivity to keep improving he believes the system needs to allow farmers to pass the assets on without incurring a huge debt.

"We need to work it out to make sure it's viable for the next generation."

World.title: Dismay over 150-year-old house being reduced to rubble
World.content:
The demolition of a dilapidated 150-year-old mansion in Launceston, in Tasmania's north, has prompted questions about gaps in heritage protection.

The Victorian-era home was earmarked for heritage listing over two decades ago, but was never placed on the State Heritage Register.

The loss of the property at 180 George Street has sparked anger and disappointment among locals and one heritage advocate who labelled the destruction as "scandalous".

The dilapidated home pictured in 2023 when owners were seeking $4 million for the sale. (Supplied)

Prior to demolition, the Launceston City Council sought the advice of heritage Tasmania, which said the property "did not demonstrate heritage values at a state level and therefore was not recommended to join the State Heritage Register".

A Heritage Tasmania spokesperson said this advice did not preclude the property from "demonstrating heritage values at a local level", saying "local heritage listing is a matter for the local planning authority".

The Launceston City Council did not provide comment on whether council considered it for local heritage listing.

Loading...

Without any protected status, the permit for the site to be bulldozed was approved by the Launceston City Council, which said the owner was exercising their rights.

Now, following community concerns, the council is working to identify other buildings that are unlisted, labelling them "potentially at risk".

A 'scandalous' loss for the city

Julie Judd owns a neighbouring property and said she was shocked to see the house torn down in a matter of days.

"There's no chance of getting any pieces of the material ... the pieces that were so unique to the area, we could have used to renovate some of the houses here," she said.

All that remains of the home is a pile of rubble. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

" I just feel really devastated, it's a real shame. "

She said anything new built on the site would not fit the architectural style of the rest of George Street.

"There's nothing modern at this end at all," she said.

Julie Judd moved to Launceston to buy a heritage home on one of the city's oldest streets. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Ms Judd said "people have done a really good job in Launceston to keep this environment looking so old and that's why visitors come here".

" It's just so unique, it's so beautiful. "

Victorian-era homes fill Launceston, with many George Street residences over a century old. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

President of the Heritage Protection Society of Tasmania, Lionel Morell, said the destruction was "scandalous".

"It's long been recognised by the National Trust as being one of the many hundreds of buildings in Launceston that had yet to be listed on the council's heritage list," he said.

In 2003, heritage architect Paul Davies was engaged by the Tasmanian Heritage Council and the Launceston City Council to undertake the Launceston Heritage Study.

The study summarised that 180 George Street complied with three of the seven criteria, with only one of them needed to enter a place on the Tasmanian Heritage Register.

The house, pictured in 2023, had renovations approved by council in 2024, before being re-listed for sale in 2025 and demolished this year. (ABC News: Damien McIntyre)

Doesn't meet the threshold

The five-bedroom property, which was advertised as a "landmark home ... ready for restoration and refinement", was sold in February this year.

The Launceston City Council said when they received the application for the property to be knocked down, they turned to Heritage Tasmania to see if an emergency listing was required.

"Heritage Tasmania subsequently advised that the property did not meet the threshold for state-level heritage listing and was therefore not recommended for inclusion on the Tasmanian Heritage Register," Mayor Matthew Garwood said.

Matthew Garwood said council sought the advice of Heritage Tasmania, before approving the owner's request for demolition. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

While Heritage Tasmania told council the property was not deemed to be of state significance, a spokesperson said this advice did not preclude the property from demonstrating heritage values at a local level.

"Local heritage listing is a matter for the local planning authority," a Heritage Tasmania spokesperson said.

In an email sent to local councillors in March, a city executive states council aims to present a planning scheme amendment to the council later this year, to avoid a repeat of this situation.

"It has now been identified that several unlisted properties, including places similar to 180 George Street, are potentially at risk," it states.

"We recognise concern around this potential building loss, and we are prioritising action to protect other at-risk heritage buildings."

George Street is a historic precinct with 65 townhouses, cottages, and commercial buildings heritage listed on the street. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

How did this happen?

Dr Stuart King, a senior lecturer in architectural design and history at the University of Melbourne, said there are different levels of heritage significance and different criteria.

The current owner purchased the property in February this year. (Supplied)

"Is the place important to telling an aspect of the area's history? Is there some high level of creative or technical achievement? Is it the building that represents a broader class of buildings?" Dr King said.

"There are other factors that might be of significance around aesthetics, associations with important people in the history of the place or with important or strong community cultural groups and so forth."

Dr Stuart King says the public can come forward and nominate buildings to be added to heritage registers. (Supplied)

Dr King said it was important to recognise the importance of historic buildings before it was too late, and described the loss of the George Street home as "disappointing".

"Launceston is one of Australia's oldest cities that had a lot of development during the 19th century ... and Launceston's been lucky to be able to retain a lot of it into the 21st century," he said.

" These types of events really bring heritage into the focus and it is a reminder that a lot of these places are really important to community and that we do all need to play a part in protecting them. "

In 2023, real estate advertising for a potential buyer attracted attention after digitally enhanced images were used to purportedly show what the house "could look like when restored to its former glory".

World.title: Cuba accepts offer of $140m in American aid, Rubio says
World.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Cuba has accepted an offer of $US100 million ($140 million) in aid but warned that a negotiated settlement between the countries is "not high".

Washington has stepped up its pressure campaign against the island's communist government in recent days, with US President Donald Trump pushing for "regime change" in Cuba.

Cuba has publicly only said that it was reviewing the aid offer made by Mr Rubio, and tensions have risen after the United States on Wednesday indicted the country's influential former president Raúl Castro on murder charges.

"They say they've accepted it," Mr Rubio told reporters in Miami about the aid offer.

But he added that the US would not allow the aid to flow into the country without controls.

"We're not going to do humanitarian aid that falls into the hands of their military company that they have. And then they take that stuff, and they sell it at the dollar stores and put the money in their pocket," Mr Rubio said.

An oil blockade of Cuba has triggered frequent blackouts on the island nation. (Reuters: Norlys Perez)

Mr Rubio, a Cuban-American and vociferous critic of the communist government in Havana, said that the United States was hoping to avoid the use of force.

The indictment in Miami of Mr Raúl over a 1996 downing of two aircraft raised speculation that President Donald Trump could use the charges as a pretext to attack the island and seize him.

"The president always has the option to do whatever it takes to support and protect the national interest and national security of the United States," Mr Rubio said.

"That said, our preference is always a diplomatic solution," he said.

"I'm just being honest with you, you know, the likelihood of that happening, given who we're dealing with right now, is not high.

"But if they have a change of heart, you know, we're here. And in the meantime, we'll keep doing what we need to do."

Raúl Castro was last seen in public on May 1 at a May Day parade in Havana. (AP: Ramon Espinosa)

But Mr Rubio also made clear he believed Cuba posed a threat.

"Cuba not only has weapons that they've acquired from Russia and China over the years, but they also host a Russian and Chinese intelligence presence in their country, not far from where we're standing right now," he said.

"So Cuba has always posed a national security threat to the United States."

Supreme Court makes ruling over US assets

Mr Rubio's comments came on the same day the US Supreme Court ruled businesses could sue for compensation in a case that stemmed from the Cuban government's decision to seize American assets in 1959.

The justices, in an 8-1 ruling, set aside a lower court's decision to throw out the judgments against Carnival, Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings, Royal Caribbean Cruises and MSC Cruises, which were sued by a US company that had built the port facilities before the Cuban revolution.

The company filed suit under the Helms-Burton Act. This 1996 law allows US nationals who owned property in Cuba to sue anyone who "traffics in property which the Cuban Government confiscated on or after January 1, 1959."

Havana Docks Corporation, which built docks at Havana's port in the early 20th century, sued under the Helms-Burton Act, seeking compensation from the cruise lines whose ships have used the terminal.

Shortly after coming to power, former leader Fidel Castro nationalised and expropriated property held by US companies, including Havana Docks, which had a 99-year concession for the construction and operation of piers at the port of Havana, granted in 1934 by Cuba's government.

Cuba has never paid any compensation to Havana Docks, but the Helms-Burton Act gave the company an opening to sue for damages in US court.

The Supreme Court ruling means those four cruise operators face $US440 million in combined judgments.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Sydney council slaps dog walkers and gender reveals with new park fees
World.content:
Pop-up picnic vendors, dog walkers and those planning a gender reveal will soon be forced to pay hundreds to use public parks, as a cash-strapped Sydney council attempts to claw its way out of millions in debt.

Under North Sydney Council's commercial and group use of public open space policy, which was adopted in March, charges and permit requirements will apply to more than 20 parks and reserves.

Proposed fees include a $300 annual permit for dog walkers, while weddings and gender reveals that require "the structured use of public open space for a defined purpose" could pay upwards of $2,000 for every three hours that the parklands are used.

It could cost upwards of $2,000 to hold a gender reveal at Bradfield park under the proposed fees. (ABC News: Daniel Guia)

Social gatherings of more than 21 people will also have to fork out between $30 to $50 and groups of up to 100 people will be required to pay between $150 and $500.

The proposed fee structure will be voted on next month, following the end of the public consultation period last Sunday.

The set fees will then come into effect at sites including Blues Point Reserve, Bradfield Park, Balls Head Reserve and Forsyth Park on July 1, with pricing to fluctuate depending on whether the location is in high demand.

Cr Baker says the new policy will help manage and balance limited public space in the area. (ABC News: Daniel Guia)

North Sydney Mayor Zoë Baker told the ABC feedback from both residents and commercial operators was mostly positive, but some vendors claimed they had been left confused by the process.

For the last five years, Vicki Ryvchin has been running pop-up picnics in the North Sydney area to celebrate special occasions ranging from marriage proposals to baby showers.

The mum-of-three said she only found out about the proposed fees through a group chat with other small businesses, and fears the proposed fee structure could "kill an entire industry".

Ms Ryvchin has been running pop-up picnics in the North Sydney area for around five years. (Supplied)

Under council's draft fees and charges, Ms Ryvchin would be required to pay $50 to $70, per three hours, for every two-person picnic she holds, in addition to a $300 annual permit to operate.

For a group of 10, she could be paying up to $200 per three hours depending on whether the park is on the foreshore or suburban.

"We're happy to pay a higher annual fee and prove our public liability year-on-year... but it's the per-event charges that are completely unreasonable and unjustified," she said.

" People want to be outside, all we're doing is just facilitating a picnic … [and] encouraging people to use our beautiful spaces that everybody pays taxes for. "

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Miriah Davis.

A council swimming in debt

The redevelopment of North Sydney Olympic Pool will cost $122 million. (AAP: Bianca De Marchii)

North Sydney Council has been trying to recoup debt from the redevelopment of North Sydney Olympic Pool, which has ballooned in cost from $56 million to $122 million.

To raise extra revenue, the council sought to increase rates by 87 per cent, but in May last year the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART) knocked back the move, ruling it had failed to make a compelling case for the steep rise.

The unsuccessful bid led the council to explore other avenues of cash flow, including charging for vantage points to view the New Year's Eve fireworks, as well as encouraging wealthy private schools in the area to pay rates on land they own.

Zoë Baker acknowledged North Sydney Council's financial fragility, but says it is also a response to complaints about park use made by residents. (YouTube: North Sydney Council)

Cr Baker said it was well documented that the council was in a "fragile financial situation".

"I can understand some individual commercial operators can be upset that they're no longer getting the use of that public open space for free," she said.

She told the ABC the new fees were projected to draw in $200,000 per year in extra revenue, but that sum did "not come close" to the current maintenance budget for North Sydney's open spaces.

According to council's draft operational plan for 2025-26, annual maintenance and operations costs for parks and gardens cost $10 million; these fees are also included in rates.

Blues Point Reserve is a hotspot for pop-up picnics due to its picturesque views of Sydney Harbour. (ABC News: Daniel Guia)

She said North Sydney had no formal policy in place to manage and balance the use of limited public open spaces, unlike Lane Cove and Mosman councils.

She said a charge to contribute towards the maintenance of public spaces was in line with IPART's suggestion that all areas of revenue be explored when it rejected council's special rate variation last year.

The council had also received "very high levels" of complaints about the impact of commercial dog walkers, boot camps, and in particular private picnics and weddings, she said.

" This isn't really just a revenue-raising process, this is also very heavily aimed at being able to manage the demand in the parks and making certain that everyone gets access to the foreshore, that it isn't always being privatised effectively. "

New fees 'poor timing' for small businesses

Chris Hanwell runs a dog walking business and uses parks in North Sydney. (Supplied)

Chris Hanwell, who runs a small dog walking business, said the introduction of the new fees was "not great timing" with the cost-of-living crisis.

"To just introduce an extra additional cost on top of all those other things seems a bit like [they're] not reading the room particularly well," he said of council's decision.

Mr Hanwell said he also paid for permits to use parks on the northern beaches and Mosman, which could cost between $500 and $2,000.

He said he could understand a small fee for amenities like dog poo bags, but was concerned the proposed fee could continue to rise each year.

Paige is unsure of how the new fees and permits will be enforced without spending big on administration costs. (Supplied)

Paige Montgomery said she was unsure how the fees would be enforced as she had not heard further information since submitting her feedback.

"It's going to cost them more in administration, in manpower, to regulate this," she said.

"I don't think it is even a business-savvy idea on their part."

Pop-up picnic providers like Paige will be forced to pay for an annual permit and fork out a fee for each job. (Supplied)

Limited space and alternate solutions

Miriam Williams, a senior lecturer in geography and planning at Macquarie University, said a permit system could actually make it easier for council to regulate the use of open spaces.

"From a planning perspective, when there's quite a demand for public space, and you have people who are earning income from the use of public space, potentially causing ongoing wear and tear and restricting the use of that public space from the broader public, then it makes sense to have a permit system," she said.

She said an ideal solution would be to find ways to incorporate new public space in the construction of new developments or existing sites.

Dr Williams said high density areas could be "tricky", although an example would look like transforming the top level of a car park into a market or plaza.

"It is often through the planning system, through agreements with developers who are developing large high rises, to put some of the land aside for open access public space."

World.title: Optus planned for 13-day outage but forgot to tell town's customers
World.content:
Lorraine Withers has been nervously waiting for the phone to ring with the results of some recent medical tests.

But because she's an Optus customer living in Coleambally in southern NSW, that's unlikely to happen any time soon.

On Monday, service to around 250 residents in the town of just over 1,000 people was cut without warning.

"I'm stressing about whether the doctors are going to be able to get in touch with me or I'm going to be able to get in touch with them," Ms Withers said.

"I'm just disappointed in them not letting us know what was happening and not letting us know that it was going to take 10 days before we could have our phones back, have our data back on our phone because … that's our lifeline out here."

Lorraine Withers is waiting on an important phone call from her doctor. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

Ms Withers said the only communication she got from the telco was a text a few months ago stating there could be some disruptions this week.

She said there was nothing to suggest a total outage lasting more than a week.

"There was no, 'It's going to take 10 days'. So I automatically said, 'It'll take a day like it normally does.'''

Optus has apologised to the Coleambally community for failing to notify residents about the outage, which is now expected to last 13 days.

The main street of Coleambally, a small town in the NSW Riverina. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

Impact on critical services

The town's medical centre also uses Optus, and a staff member, Sam Harris, said they had no idea about the outage.

"It was phone and internet that were impacted, so on the doctor's computer, we couldn't do scripts," she said.

"Ringing patients with results is my job.

" I can't get onto them … I can't ring them to tell them the doctor needs to see them, so I'm going to have to drive to them because they need to be seen personally. "

The medical centre has now purchased a satellite internet service to reconnect their phone to wi-fi, but many patients are still unable to call them.

Ms Harris said she was especially concerned for some of the elderly residents in town.

Sam Harris works at the town's medical centre and she said patients were unable to contact the centre as soon as the outage began. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

"We've got a lot of elderly people at home panicking because they can't make a phone call," she said.

"Yes, they can ring Triple Zero, but they can't ring family, they can't ring for help.

"Mail ladies having to travel to Narrandera, they can't ring if they break down and their option is to ring Triple Zero, and that's just not good enough."

An Optus spokesperson said Triple Zero calls could still be made.

"Calls to emergency services will connect via other mobile networks where coverage is available, noting there may be a delay while the connection transfers," the spokesperson said.

It comes after the telco faced backlash over outages in remote areas, which led to problems with contacting Triple Zero.

The local service station told ABC it was the only business in town that stocked SIM cards.

It said the few Telstra prepaid SIMs in stock when the outage hit sold out that same day.

SIM cards for other networks have almost sold out in town. (ABC News: Nicola Ceccato)

The Murrumbidgee Shire Council also said it was not notified.

An Optus spokesperson has apologised for the lack of communication and said planned customer notifications were not issued due to a technical issue ahead of the work.

The provider said it was rebuilding the service tower to improve "network performance and reliability" and that completion was expected by May 30.

However, following community concerns, an Optus spokesperson said they are working to bring the completion date forward and were deploying temporary mobile infrastructure for interim coverage, which is expected to be operational by Saturday.

Optus has said that for affected customers, they are waiving monthly mobile access fees for three months.

It comes at the same time that Optus' owner, Singtel, announced on Thursday that it's looking to sell a minority stake in the telco.

Ms Withers said the situation had affected her trust in the service for future use.

"It's sad that we're being forgotten," she said.

"That's what it feels like, it feels like they don't care."

World.title: Why consumers are forking out more for whiting, calamari and garfish
World.content:
South Australia's peak seafood body says a short supply of some species due to the algal bloom and commercial fishing restrictions has led to slight price increases, as it warns it could take industry five to 10 years to fully recover.

Meanwhile, one seafood retailer says prices for some premium fish, such as King George Whiting which currently costs $99.99 online, have remained high.

Gulf St Vincent was closed for commercial marine scalefish fishing in November last year after the bloom devastated fish stocks, including popular species like southern calamari, King George Whiting and garfish.

The restricted area was scheduled to reopen in July this year, but the closure has been extended until May 2027 due to depleted numbers.

Seafood Industry SA executive officer Kyri Toumazos says Gulf St Vincent is a "highly productive" area and is responsible for approximately 50 per cent of the state's production of marine scalefish, especially garfish, whiting and calamari.

He says while the extended closure is crucial for the gulf's long-term sustainability, there is a chance it could increase prices further.

Kyri Toumazos says some fish are more expensive than usual. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"That is always a risk when you have less supply," Mr Toumazos said.

"There's definitely been a shorter supply of seafood over the last few months … some species, definitely we've seen a slight [price] increase, such as calamari and whiting are the two that are predominantly the drivers here in South Australia.

"Garfish, we've seen a little bit of a [price] increase, but garfish usually is a product that gets caught at different times of the year so we're hoping that over the next few months we will see greater catches.

"We are working with our local fishers to ensure that all our local produce gets first opportunity to be consumed here in South Australia and we're hoping that we've seen the worst of it so far."

Heartbreak of toxic algal bloom outbreak A mysterious, brown foam appeared on a beach an hour south of Adelaide. It was just the beginning of a toxic algal bloom that has now grown to thousands of square kilometres in size, killing precious sea life in its wake. Experts say it could be a sign of things to come.

Mr Toumazos said the Gulf St Vincent closure, in addition to restrictions in the Spencer Gulf, has added pressure on the state's other fishing zones to supplement lower supply.

He says it comes at a time when the fishing industry is also grappling with rising fuel and operating costs.

"At the moment, everything seems to be very stable in those areas, so we are continuing with our current management, but we are monitoring it extensively throughout the next few months," he said.

"There is an extensive part of our coastline that is not impacted by algal bloom, especially west of Port Lincoln, and those areas are productive areas for fish across calamari, blue swimmer crab, and whiting."

He said it while was encouraging that some species — such as the blue swimmer crab — have been able to recover quickly in numbers, it could take five to 10 years for the industry to return to pre-bloom capacity.

"That is without another re-occurrence of a bloom or the traces of the bloom continuing as we're seeing in Spencer Gulf for long periods of time," Mr Toumazos said.

" All experts are telling us do not expect a linear increase in stocks. It's going to be a bouncy road ahead. "

'We haven't had the abundance of fish'

At the Adelaide Central Market, seafood company Angelakis Brothers director Alex Knoll said the bloom has impacted the availability and variety of species that customers expect this time of year.

Alex Knoll said some species are in short supply, pushing prices up. (ABC News: Rachael Merritt)

"We would normally start to see an abundance of King George Whiting come through the markets, that's not happening at the moment but we are getting some good numbers of garfish," Mr Knoll said.

"It will be a little bit harder for the South Australian squid but there is always an alternative available which I think is really important.

"Garfish has come through in larger numbers, and we are seeing that market price coming down again now, although it has been quite high for quite a while now."

Mr Knoll said while it's not uncommon to see a premium species like King George Whiting retail for nearly $100 per kilogram, especially around Christmas time, prices have remained high.

"I guess it's been sustained for a lot longer because we haven't had the abundance of fish coming out of the water so we can then reduce the price," he said.

Alternatives on the menu

Some SA seafood producers and sellers reported a drop in sales and consumer confidence last year due to perceptions over the algal bloom, despite a state government campaign reassuring people local seafood in stores was safe to eat.

A government education campaign about the safety of SA seafood continues. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

The government's latest water testing shows low or zero levels of karenia were recorded across most of the coastline.

Elevated levels were recorded at six sites on the Eyre Peninsula, one site on the Yorke Peninsula and Spencer Gulf.

Fair Seafood owner Amanda Prance said the changes in supply provide a chance to educate customers on alternate species they may not be familiar with.

Amanda Prance says in a cost-of-living crisis, consumers can choose from a range of species at different price points. (ABC News: Rachael Merritt)

"We can't support the fishers that are in these regions so we're obviously using other fishermen outside of those regions for our produce … and that means different species," she said.

"We haven't had King George Whiting in for probably about four weeks … and we enjoy it when we get it in but it's not our primary focus.

"If you want to do a curry, if you want to put something on the barbecue, if you want to have a pan fry, we've always got a fish available for that.

"Particularly with cost of living, that's obviously a consideration … we always try and make sure we've got fish in those different price points."

World.title: Sweeping cuts but little detail — can the government stick to the Abetz budget?
World.content:
Since Eric Abetz became Tasmania's treasurer nine months ago, there have been two prevailing questions.

How much will be cut? And what will be cut?

He's delivered on the first question.

The 2026-27 year's $600 million operating deficit is an improvement on the $923 million estimated deficit for the current year.

The rubber really hits the road in 2027-28 when he's hoping to record a surplus.

But what has he cut?

We don't really know.

Eric Abetz says the government will "maintain frontline services" in the healthcare system, but will make cuts of $700 million. (Pixabay: CC0)

The financial turnaround is dependent on $1.47 billion in "operational efficiencies".

The treasurer has pointed to the back-end of the public service as the main target for cuts, eyeing off 1,700 jobs in the next four years.

"Did we have an appropriate bureaucracy prior to COVID? I think most people would say 'yes,'" he said.

"So, trying to right-size the bureaucracy to our income is something that is doable".

But $1.47 billion sounds like a tall order.

The government is seeking operational efficiency cuts of $228 million from the education department over four years. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

Look through the individual chapters and you won't find much more detail.

To cut its $131 million this year, the Department of Health will review fees and charges, increase its focus on lowering locum and agency costs and revise its executive structure.

The Justice Department will remove one deputy secretary position and invest in digital and AI solutions and a few other actions for $7.5 million in savings.

Where are the cuts coming from in Tasmania's state budget? Treasurer Eric Abetz wants to find $1.47 billion in "efficiencies" in Tasmania's state budget. This is what's on the chopping block.

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment will consolidate office accommodation and streamline training delivery to find $5 million this year.

Is there genuinely $1.47 billion worth of deputy secretaries doing nothing and wasted office accommodation that can be scrapped without affecting frontline services?

If the answer is yes, that's almost more troubling.

Australian Education Union branch president David Genford is none the wiser about how the government's reaching those targets.

"It's very difficult to know. I can't get a straight answer," he said.

"We're told there will be streamlining of services. There's not 155 jobs that can be simply cleared up like that."

The truth is, it will be nigh on impossible to entirely protect frontline services from $1.47 billion in cuts.

From the government's promise of "no cuts" to frontline services two years ago, the treasurer could only promise yesterday that they'll be "maintained".

The budget book itself goes even further, saying only that "consideration will be given to minimising impacts on frontline service delivery".

Cuts kept under wraps

This year's budget continues a trend of the government making "efficiency" its main savings method.

Four years ago, then-treasurer Michael Ferguson reintroduced the efficiency dividend. Last year, Guy Barnett founded the EPU (efficiency and productivity unit).

Those efficiency measures have become less and less about keeping budgets in check and more about the main game.

Putting all those savings under one broad budget line also keeps them under wraps.

"Operational efficiency" is a lot easier reading than "closing schools" or "closing wards".

By not painting a specific target on its back, the government can avoid a backlash.

Take last week's federal budget. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers are facing some opposition to their tax changes.

They're now in a fight over not just breaking an election promise, but having to explain the impact on small businesses.

Former treasurer Guy Barnett flagged asset sales in last year's state budget.

Three weeks later, that was listed as a reason for a no-confidence motion in Premier Jeremy Rockliff.

Upon returning to government, Mr Barnett was no longer treasurer and asset sales were off the table.

But given the scale of these cuts, shouldn't we get to see them?

Jess Munday says the decisions on where to cut are being pushed onto the public sector. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Unions Tasmania secretary Jessica Munday called on the government to explain further.

"This is another case of the government pushing responsibility onto the public sector to make decisions about where to cut," she said.

" I'd like to know, and I think Tasmanians deserve to know, which school is it, Eric? Which hospital? Which park? Which service that we rely on? Which Service Tasmania is not going to be there? "

It's a lot harder to mobilise a campaign against operational efficiencies.

But there is $1.47 billion worth of bad press to come.

Can the state hit budget targets?

Credit rating agency S&P Global, which recently revised down Tasmania's credit rating from AA+ to AA said the "ambitious" budget "hinges on execution".

"We believe the state will find it difficult to hit its targets given rising spending pressures, demographic obstacles, and limited revenue-generating capacity," the agency said in a statement following the budget's delivery.

Economist Saul Eslake, who was bullish on this budget, said people were entitled to be sceptical that the government could reach these targets.

But he said the Abetz budget was clearer than previous ones about how the money would be saved.

" I suspect Mr Abetz will be more determined to impose discipline on his ministerial colleagues and departments than his predecessors have been. "

Onus on departments to identify where to cut

This is a government that routinely overshoots its expenditure targets (it did by about $132 million last year) and is saved by lower-than-forecast infrastructure spending and higher-than-expected GST payments from the federal government.

It's also tied one arm behind its back in refusing to consider any new revenue, though the fees and charges review mentioned in the budget will be worth watching.

The treasurer has laid out the plan.

It's now the responsibility of the entire cabinet, and the departments themselves, to stick to it.

It is tough to believe that this will not have an impact on frontline services. Will those cuts really be followed through on?

The Police, Fire and Emergency Department will need to find $72 million in operational efficiencies. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

Sugar-hit spending will need to be resisted.

There's also an election scheduled for 2029, just as the treasurer is promising peak net debt.

This budget includes $244 million worth of election commitments from last year's snap state election, which was deemed more restrained than usual.

How much will the next one cost and will it be any different from the previous spend-a-thons?

The treasurer indicated in the budget lock-up that the message had sunk in.

He said there was an "absolute determination" to meet those targets.

Former treasurers have stood there before and promised a surplus was on the way, for it to never eventuate.

Will this time be any different?

World.title: 'Stuck between two psychopaths': Cubans describe life as country goes dark
World.content:
The colourful charm of Cuba's capital, Havana, has long made it a magnet for tourists from abroad.

That's why Betty* decided to start a tour guide business after moving there a couple of years ago.

Betty had been forced to leave her home city, further inland, because power blackouts had become crippling. Sometimes, the electricity was out for 16 hours a day.

Her tourism business became the main source of income for her family.

But now, as the US blocks oil shipments to Cuba and power constantly goes out across the country, the tourism industry is "all but dead", she says.

"You can no longer find streets packed with travellers, music and dance," Betty told the ABC.

"Only Cuban nationals, still attempting to take some bread home."

Some homes in Cuba have been without a water supply for months. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Poor sanitation is contributing to the spread of disease. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Cuba has been subject to punishing American sanctions since 1960, shortly after Fidel Castro and his forces took power and seized foreign assets.

In the months leading up to this week's arrest warrant for Fidel Castro's brother, former president Raúl Castro, the Trump administration intensified the pressure campaign.

The US has maintained an effective blockade of energy to Cuba since January, when it threatened tariffs on any country that provided oil.

It had already stopped Venezuelan oil exports after toppling that country's leader, Nicolás Maduro, in January.

Mexico had been a major supplier. By early February, it had halted its shipments.

One Russian oil tanker was allowed through the US blockade at the end of March, easing the crisis for about a month.

Those supplies are now exhausted.

Russia has sent another tanker, but it's not clear if it will be allowed to dock.

Havana bears the signs of decades of neglect. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Prices have rocketed, and many businesses have closed. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

For now, Betty travels around Havana to friends' homes who might have power, so she can use the internet to try to reach potential foreign visitors.

"Old Havana, once the main hub of visitors, is but a ghost town," she said

"Prices have skyrocketed for the only still-standing businesses to stay afloat."

'One of the dirtiest cities in Latin America'

Betty is plagued by another worry: a toothache that she says hospitals will be unable to address due to a lack of power and supplies.

She is searching for treatment options on the black market, as Cuba's healthcare system plunges deeper into crisis.

UN officials estimate there are 100,000 patients, including 11,000 children, waiting for surgeries delayed by power and supply shortages.

Mosquito-borne and water-borne diseases are spreading. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

There are few cars on the road, and getting around is becoming more difficult. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Sewage infrastructure is breaking down, causing disease. Mosquitoes are spreading illness, too.

Francisco, who lives just east of Havana in an area called Alamar, said both he and his wife had been infected with the debilitating mosquito-borne chikungunya virus. Both had also had hepatitis A.

"I dare say that Havana has become one of the dirtiest cities in Latin America," Francisco said.

"Another very serious problem is garbage collection.

"Without fuel, the garbage isn't being collected. More than a month goes by without collection, and the townspeople, in protest, start burning it."

Where he lives, the electricity supply has dwindled to just six hours a day, three in the morning and three at night.

Cuba has been under a US embargo since 1960. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Many Cubans are now wondering what the US will do next. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Bracing for a summer of blackouts

Summer is now setting in in tropical Cuba.

The heat means food wastes in refrigerators with no power supply.

Lucia, who lives in a neighbourhood in central Havana, says it is getting harder for people to sleep at night.

"Sometimes when it's like 20 hours of blackouts, it's all night long," she said.

"There are mosquitoes in the night. I think that's why people are so stressed, because they're not able to sleep.

"If you go walking by the street, you can hear people talking, and everybody's talking about the same subject … how hard it is, how many hours without electricity."

Cuba experiences intense summers. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Across the country, power supplies have become intermittent and unreliable. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Before the US blockade, she said, the power crisis was more manageable.

"There were already a lot of blackouts, but it was more organised, if I can say.

"Every neighbourhood [block] had a schedule, so you know when you were going to have light, like, four hours a day, four hours yes, four hours no."

The US says Cuba is a national security threat.

The Trump order that threatened tariffs on its oil suppliers pointed to the regime's collaboration with Chinese and Russian intelligence, among others.

The Trump administration ultimately wants regime change.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said some sort of diplomatic solution was "our preference", but "the likelihood of that happening, given who we're dealing with, is not high".

In a Spanish-language video message addressing Cubans this week, he said: "The real reason you don't have electricity, fuel or food is because those who control your country have plundered billions of dollars, but nothing has been used to help the people."

Without oil, few cars are on the road and public transport has essentially stopped working. A new wave of tuktuk drivers is replacing it.

Tuktuks are replacing other forms of transport. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Petrol supplies have been cut off. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

But Lucia says the hardest part of the crisis is the lack of water. Her building's water supply has been cut off for six months.

She walks half a block to fill a bucket for cooking and showering, lugging the water up several floors to her apartment. The supplies run out quickly, so people have to get up early or miss out.

"You can live without electricity," Lucia said, "but living without water is just not possible."

Protesters risk brutal punishment

Sporadic and small protests broke out last week as the island's energy reserves ran out.

It was a sign of just how desperate people had become, says Havana-born Sebastian Arcos, who is now the interim director of the Institute for Cuban Studies at Florida International University (FIU).

"This is a police state, a totalitarian society. Political opposition, particularly open political opposition, is severely punished," he said.

Many Cubans say political change is urgent. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Cubans are split on the prospect of US intervention, but many believe sanctions should continue. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Particularly notable were the protests in Havana, where Mr Arcos says the regime conducts the most surveillance.

"That unwritten contract between a totalitarian society and the population where totalitarians say, 'We're going to take away your freedoms but at least we're going to give you the basic standards of living,' in Cuba, it's gone, it's disappeared," he says.

"[The regime] has shown over the last 30 years that they are willing to sacrifice the welfare of the Cuban population in order to remain in power."

Cubans have become "cannon fodder" in a conflict between two governments, one expert says. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

UN officials believe 100,000 people are waiting for surgeries that have been postponed. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

The restrictions on free speech mean public opinion is difficult to accurately measure.

In one recent online survey, which attracted 42,000 voluntary responses, 94 per cent of respondents living in Cuba said political change was urgent.

Fifty-six per cent expressed support for US military intervention, and more than three-quarters said the US embargo should stay in place, either in whole or in part.

Support for the US embargo and military intervention was even stronger among the surveyed diaspora.

'Stuck between two psychopaths'

Michael Bustamante, a Cuba expert at Florida University, says the Cuban people have become "cannon fodder" in a conflict between two governments that has been running for some 70 years.

"It's absolutely heartbreaking what they're enduring in this moment," he said.

"I can't imagine having to wake up at three in the morning because the lights are going to come on for an hour, that's the hour I'm going to have to cook what little food hasn't already gone rotten in my refrigerator.

"It's the Cuban people that are bearing the brunt of the effects both of incredible economic coercion from the United States, but also years and years of a lack of internal reform."

Daily life continues amid the uncertainty. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Many Cubans have grown up under totalitarian rule. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

Lucia describes the situation as "like being stuck between two psychopaths".

"I feel very angry to both sides, to be honest."

She thinks the US hopes of a civil uprising are unrealistic.

"In other countries, for much less than what's happening here, people go out to the streets and protest," she said.

"Here I think people are very scared, and I think they just don't have faith in the possibility of making something change that way."

But she also wants the US to stay out.

"I don't really want the US to come here. I don't think they really care about democracy or our liberty or something. I think they have other interests.

"If somebody cared about democracy or human rights or whatever, they would have already done something."

* Names have been changed.

About 10 million people live in Cuba. (ABC News: Harvey Lujes)

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Second group of IS-linked families leave Syria for Australia, according to reports; Iran war and inflation hit jobs market as unemployment surges
World.content:
A second group of Australian women and children with Islamic State links have left a camp in north-east Syria to return home, the ABC reports.

Overnight, the ABC reported witnessing buses at the al-Roj refugee camp to take the group to Damascus for onward flights.

Members of Australian families at al-Roj camp in eastern Syria preparing to leave to return to Australia last month. AP

Earlier this month, four women and nine children returned to Australia after spending years at the camp. Three of the women were arrested upon arrival and are separately facing charges including being a member of a terrorist organisation and crimes against humanity.

A total of 34 Australian women and children first attempted to leave the camp in February, but were turned back around 50 kilometres down the road.

World.title: Airbus, Air France found guilty of manslaughter over crash that killed 228 people
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Airbus, Air France found guilty of manslaughter over crash that killed 228 people Tim Hepher May 22, 2026 — 6:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: A French appeals court found Airbus and Air France guilty of corporate manslaughter over the Rio-Paris plane crash, but a 17-year legal battle over the country’s worst aviation disaster is set to continue. “Justice has absolutely been done,” Daniele Lamy, president of the AF447 victims’ association, whose son was one of 228 people who died in the crash, said outside the courtroom. The trial exposed bitter divisions between the airline and planemaker over the cause of the accident and a gulf between a civil crash report that focused mainly on the actions of pilots and a wider chain of cause and effect highlighted by the court. Bloomberg Relatives of some of those who died when the Airbus A330 plunged in pitch darkness into the Atlantic during an equatorial storm on June 1, 2009, listened to the verdict in silence. A lower court had in 2023 cleared the two French companies, both of which have repeatedly denied the charges.



Related Article Aviation It’s two years since a Singapore Airlines flight hit horror turbulence. Investigators just released their report Thursday’s verdict is the latest milestone in a legal marathon involving relatives of the mainly French, Brazilian and German victims and two of France’s most emblematic companies. The appeals court ordered them both to pay the maximum fine for corporate manslaughter, €225,000 ($365,420), following the request of prosecutors during last year’s eight-week trial. The fines, amounting to just a few minutes of either company’s revenue, have been widely dismissed as a token penalty but families said corporate reputations were on the line. Airbus and Air France both said they would appeal to France’s highest court, ignoring pleas from the relatives.



“There is no human, moral or legal justification in continuing this procedure,” said Lamy, who appealed to both companies to stop what she called “procedural harassment”. Lawyers had predicted further appeals on legal points and warned these could potentially drag the process out for years. Hundreds of people died when an Airbus A330 plunged into the Atlantic in 2009 during an equatorial storm. AP Families’ lawyer Alain Jakubowicz told Reuters a second full re-trial, rehashing the evidence a third time, could not be ruled out if the Court of Cassation faulted Thursday’s verdict. Relatives and lawyers sat in a high-windowed courtroom that has witnessed some of France’s most historic trials as a judge read out a list of victims, many sharing the same family names.



The black boxes from Flight 447 were retrieved in 2011, after a two-year deep-sea search that was almost called off. ‘Justice has absolutely been done.’ Daniele Lamy, president of the AF447 victims’ association The trial exposed bitter divisions between the airline and planemaker over the cause of the accident and a gulf between a civil crash report that focused mainly on the actions of pilots and a wider chain of cause and effect highlighted by the court. Analysts said the ruling was unlikely to alter regulators’ views on the crash, which did not lead to major technical changes. France’s BEA crash investigators found the plane’s crew had pushed their jet into a stall, chopping lift from under the wings, after mishandling a problem to do with iced-up sensors.



Related Article Aviation United Airlines jet just avoids ‘catastrophe’ after hitting a bakery truck and pole while landing Prosecutors, however, focused their attention on alleged failures inside both the planemaker and airline. Those included poor training and failing to follow up on earlier sensor flaws. To prove manslaughter, prosecutors had to not only establish negligence but also pull the threads together to demonstrate how this caused the crash. Their failure to make that part of the argument stick had resulted in the earlier acquittal. Lamy said the deceased pilots had been “rehabilitated”. Reuters The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to advance, Wall Street seesaws as oil prices swing
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to advance, Wall Street seesaws as oil prices swing Stan Choe Updated May 22, 2026 — 6:13am ,first published 5:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wall Street has closed a choppy session higher after hour-to-hour swings for oil prices keep jerking financial markets around. The S&P 500 rose 0.2 per cent and inched closer to its all-time high set last week. The Dow Jones added 276.3 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.1 per cent higher. The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures at 5.53am AEST pointing to a rise of 36 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX surged by 1.5 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.49¢. Bond market pressure on Wall Street is continuing to ease. AP All three indexes erased early drops and gained strength following the latest U-turn for oil prices. Brent crude oil briefly got above $US109 per barrel in the morning, threatening to worsen the world’s already high inflation, before quickly erasing all its gains in midday trading and falling 2 per cent to $US102.93. Oil prices have been yo-yoing because of uncertainty about how long the war with Iran will keep the Strait of Hormuz shut. The closure has prevented oil tankers from exiting the Persian Gulf to deliver crude to customers worldwide, driving up oil’s price.



As oil prices eased on Thursday, so did pressure on Wall Street that’s been building from the bond market. Related Article Opinion

IPO Dreaming big: Elon Musk’s $2.5 trillion vision is about to become reality Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Yields had climbed so high that they’re threatening to slow economies worldwide and undercut prices for stocks, bitcoin and all kinds of other investments. They’ve already forced the average long-term US mortgage rate to its most expensive level since last summer, and they could curtail companies’ borrowing to build the AI data centres that have been supporting the US economy’s growth recently. The yield on the 10-year Treasury briefly got near 4.63 per cent in the morning before falling back to 4.55 per cent following the midday turnaround for oil prices. That’s down from 4.57 per cent late Wednesday and from 4.67 per cent the day before. Some of the biggest beneficiaries of lower yields can be the smallest companies, many of which need to borrow money to grow. The Russell 2000 index of the smallest US stocks rallied 1.2 per cent, far more than the rest of the market.



Stocks of companies with big fuel bills also rose because of the easing of oil prices. Southwest Airlines climbed 2.7 per cent, and American Airlines flew 4.9 per cent higher. Ralph Lauren jumped 13.8 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. They helped offset a 1.8 per cent drop for Nvidia, which is one of Wall Street’s most influential stocks because of its immense size. The chip company reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while also forecasting revenue for the current quarter that cleared analysts’ estimates. “The buildout of AI factories — the largest infrastructure expansion in human history — is accelerating at extraordinary speed,” CEO Jensen Huang said. But such performances and such talk have become routine, and Nvidia’s stock swivelled between losses and gains before falling.



Some analysts said the weakness may have been because investors were locking in profits after Nvidia’s stock had soared nearly 70 per cent over the prior year, more than double the S&P 500’s 27 per cent jump. The broad AI industry is also getting criticism for becoming too expensive, as well as too circular as Nvidia has bought ownership stakes in companies that use its own chips that drive Nvidia’s revenue. Related Article Exclusive

Media & marketing ABC chair hits back at News Corp’s ‘divisive’ antisemitism reporting Walmart also fell, 7.3 per cent, following its profit report. The retailer delivered another quarter of impressive revenue but offered up weaker forecasts for upcoming profit than analysts expected. Walmart has resonated with Americans who have grown increasingly cautious about where they spend their money with inflation taking a bigger bite out of paychecks, and discouraged about the economy. A preliminary report on US business activity suggested that companies are also feeling the bite of higher inflation.



A flash survey from S&P Global said growth in activity for US services businesses unexpectedly slowed a tad, though growth was better than forecast for U.S manufacturers. “The damaging economic impact from the war in the Middle East is becoming increasingly evident in the business surveys,” according to Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. A separate report, meanwhile, gave the latest signal that the US job market remains in better shape than economists expected. The number of US workers applying for unemployment benefits last week unexpectedly declined in an indication of fewer layoffs. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following bigger moves in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi Kospi soared 8.4 per cent thanks to strength for technology stocks. Samsung Electronics jumped 8.5 per cent after its labor union and management reached an agreement late Wednesday that averted a strike. SK Hynix, a chip company partnering with Nvidia, surged 11.2 per cent.



Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 jumped 3.1 per cent, while indexes fell 1 per cent in Hong Kong and 2 per cent in Shanghai. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
